description:
Whilst in Cebu during our first ever visit to the Philippines in May 2024, we noticed just how many Don Macchiato’s there were. We had never seen the shop before outside of the Philippines or even in Manila. But in Cebu they are absolutely everywhere. 

After a little bit of google research we found out that there are over 700 branches in The Philippines and also that it is the cheapest coffee chain in the Philippines. At just ₽39 ($0.67) for any item on their menu we just had to give it a try. When we landed back in Manila during our second visit we could not find them anywhere. We later learned it was more of a thing that was found down south. 

We spent 1 night in Puerto Princesa before heading to El Nido and whilst on a trike Jason spotted one out of the corner of his eye. This was our chance to taste the Filipino owned coffee chain. 

It was a small shop but in all honesty what did we expect, the menu is small and it is designed that way. They only have a small number of coffees on it which is great if you are easily intimated by the typically MASSIVE menu that most coffee shops have plastered on their walls. 

We went for a the famous caramel macchiato (iced and hot) it did not disappoint, for ₽39 we’d choose this over Starbucks any day!

description:
The ferry to Coron was cancelled due to a typhoon so instead, we made our way back down South to Port Barton! This wasn’t initially on our itinerary but WOW aren’t we glad we came here! Port Barton is a smaller, more rural and less developed version of El Nido and during our short stay there, we fell in love.

We visited Coconut beach after a difficult tuktuk drive there though ankle deep mud and rough roads! Coconut beach has pigs on the beach that you can stroke and play with along with numerous beautiful dogs. We spent the afternoon with the pigs, dogs and soaking up the beautiful beach and the incredible amount of coconut trees lining the sand. We would urge anybody planning their route through Palawan to include Port Barton, especially if you want to see a slower, less developed beach town. 

After we’d had our fill of one of the Philippines most beautiful beaches (in our opinion), we headed out for some dinner and found ourselves at ‘Pork Hub’ a rather precariously named roasted pork shop. We both love eating local Filipino food and roasted pork in the Philippines never disappoints so we tucked in to 2 portions of the roasted, crispy pork.

We were super unlucky with the weather in Palawan, as a typhoon forced us to change all our plans. With the ferry to Coron cancelled, we headed south to Port Barton—a hidden gem that wasn’t originally on our itinerary. Wow, are we glad we found it!

Port Barton is a quieter, more rural alternative to El Nido, with fewer tourists and a more laid-back atmosphere. Despite the rough tuktuk ride through ankle-deep mud, we made it to Coconut Beach, where we met friendly pigs, playful dogs, and relaxed under the shade of countless coconut trees. This is the perfect spot for anyone looking for a slower, more authentic beach experience in Palawan.

After enjoying the stunning beach, we discovered Pork Hub, a local roasted pork shop. Filipino roasted pork is a must-try, and it did not disappoint! We tucked into crispy, tender portions of pork—definitely one of the best meals we had during our trip.

We highly recommend adding Port Barton to your Palawan itinerary if you're looking for a quieter, less developed destination. It’s an unforgettable experience!

title: Visiting El Nido During A TYPHOON! #typhoon #elnido #philippines #filipino #palawan #travel #vlog
tags: el nido|el nido philippines|typhoon philippines|typhoon season philippines|philippines during typhoon|el nido palawan|el nido trip|philippines travel|philippines vlog|philippines travel vlog|el nido travel|el nido vlog|el nido travel vlog|what to do in el nido|philippines vlogger|travel vlogger in the philippines|filipino vlogger|travel philippines|backpacking philippines|backpacking travel vlog|backpacking vlog|outpost el nido|palawan philippines
description:
What started off as an exciting surprise trip down to El Nido soon turned into a bit of a nightmare as a typhoon hit. The typhoon primarily affected northern Philippines but we the bad weather also spread to El Nido causing heavy rains and strong winds. 

Due to this, all activities in El Nido and Coron (island hopping, boat trips, zip lines etc) were all cancelled for the duration of our stay. And no surprise, all ferries were cancelled too, meaning we were stuck in El Nido for 3 more nights than we had originally planned and our trip to Coron was completely cancelled. 

We had to reverse our journey and head back down to Puerto Princesa where we eventually got a flight back to Manila (we filmed a separate video on this to show our experience of the completely changed plans). As we didn’t get to be experience the beauty of Palawan, we will certainly be back as there is so much to see and do on this beautiful island… just not during a typhoon! 

Sending love to everybody who was affected by the typhoon. 
E&J

description:
Does the smiling Red Horse beer REALLY exist? We have been told by many Filipino people to "look out for the smiling horse" on the label of Red Horse beer, and that if we were to find this mythical beer, we would discover the rare brew that is MUCH stronger than other Red Horse beers of the same bottle. These stories/folk tales fascinated us. Did Red Horse really release a secret beer, an Easter egg, if you will, for beer drinkers and enthusiasts to hunt down?

Well, during our very rainy trip to El Nido, Philippines, we had so much spare time due to bad weather and canceled island hopping trips that we decided to begin a little treasure hunt of our own! We started our hunt where all good pirates do... on the beach of El Nido. The waves were high, but our spirits were not. We really believed this to be a "fool's errand," BUT we decided to look for this rumored beer all the same.

As we walked around the busy (and construction-filled) streets of the town, we were unsure where to begin. We asked a few of the local trike drivers if they had heard of it and, if so, where we could find it. This question was met with confusion, then laughter—almost as if we had asked these men, "Where can we find Santa Claus?" We unsuccessfully searched nearly all the shops in El Nido town before calling it a failed mission and heading back to OUTPOST HOSTEL EL NIDO.

The rain had begun to fall hard as we left our trike, and we ran across the beach to our accommodation (might we add, the bar is the first thing you are greeted with when entering this place). So, we asked the man at the bar, "Jay Z," if he had ever heard of this Happy Horse beer. He answered, "Yes, but only once in my life, and I was very young." He opened up the chest freezer behind the bar and rifled through each bottle of Red Horse until... SUCCESS!

He pulled out this bottle like a glowing chalice. We all began to laugh and smile so much (maybe that's why it's called the Happy Horse). It was so strange to see this bottle, which looked so similar to the other Red Horse beers, only with a slightly different horse on the front sporting that cheeky, infamous smile. The writing was red, and the back of the label had NO alcohol percentage number on it—something so funny/crazy to see! It's like the company was secretly saying, "Drink it, but what comes after is up to you." The taste was noticeably stronger, as if someone had poured gin into the bottle before it was capped and boxed up.

This was such a fun thing to film, as we honestly believed we were NOT going to find one. So when we did, it was all the more special.

title: Brits Explore El Nido(Palawan, Philippines)🇵🇭
tags: The Philippines|Philippines|filipino|filipino vlog|philippines Vlog|Travel vlog|travel vlog philippines|British Vloggers In The Philippines|Backpacker|Backpacker in The Philippines|Travel Vlog South East Asia|South East Asia Travel Videos|Travel Videos|Backpacking Vlog|Travel|Where to go backpacking in south east Asia|Is the Philippines safe|holiday|bloggers in the philippines|vloggers in the philippines|filipino food|filipino food vlog|filipino foodie|foodie
description:
Welcome to El Nido, the crown jewel of Palawan, Philippines! Nestled on the edge of turquoise waters, surrounded by towering limestone cliffs, and dotted with hidden lagoons and pristine beaches—this is paradise on Earth. Whether you're an adventure seeker, a beach lover, or simply looking to escape into nature, El Nido has something for everyone.

We began our trip here after a very tough drive from Puerto Princesa. We had no idea the roads would be so winding, and just one hour into this six-hour journey, I (Jason) started to feel very unwell. After we checked into our accommodation at OUTPOST HOSTEL, we pretty much just went straight to sleep, as the long drive had drained the life out of us.

On the first morning, still not feeling 100%, we headed into town. The fare for the trike ride was a flat rate of ₱100. We explored the town for a little while and noticed just how much construction was underway. Every building that wasn’t open was being renovated, and the streets had been torn up by diggers.

We wandered around for a couple of hours, saying hello to the friendly locals and stopping off at El Nido Bakery, which seemed to be very popular. While deciding what sweet treats to try, a young boy told us to avoid one of the cakes, as he had eaten it before and said it was (in his words) “very bad.” We think it was because the cake looked really appealing, with bright colors, but when he tasted it, he realized it wasn't fruity but rather just food coloring with unusual flavors. From that moment on, he vowed never to let anyone else make the same mistake.

We were then advised to try one of the donuts, filled with one of the Philippines' favorite ingredients—yes, you guessed it, Ube.

Ube (for those of you who don’t know) is a type of purple yam commonly used in Filipino cuisine. It's known for its striking, vibrant purple color and naturally sweet, nutty flavor. Ube is often used in desserts, such as ube halaya (a sweet, creamy jam-like treat), ube ice cream, and ube cake. Beyond its unique taste, it's prized for its versatility in both traditional and modern dishes. It can be boiled, mashed, or pureed, and its sweet, earthy flavor lends itself to a variety of sweet and savory applications. Ube has recently gained popularity worldwide, especially in fusion desserts and baked goods.

Our total came to only ₱25 ($0.40), which was an amazing deal for some fresh Filipino treats.

description:
During our short stay in Palawan we noticed that they started serving Lechon very late in comparison to other places we’ve been to in the Philippines! 

Lechon is a popular Filipino dish consisting of a whole pig that is roasted over an open flame or in an oven until the skin is crispy and the meat is tender and flavorful. The pig is often marinated with a blend of spices, herbs, and seasonings before being slowly roasted for several hours.

Lechon is typically served during special occasions and celebrations in the Philippines. It is a centerpiece dish at festive events like birthdays, weddings, Christmas, New Year, town fiestas, and other major gatherings. The tradition of serving lechon is associated with generosity and is seen as a symbol of abundance and celebration. It is generally served earlier in the day and when the street seller/restaurant runs out they tend to then go home. So it was very different to see it being set up at 4pm in Palawan.

title: First Time in Puerto Princesa, Why Are There No Tourists? 🇵🇭

description:
After flying in from Manila, we decided to spend one night and one full day in Puerto Princesa, Palawan's largest city. We wanted to see for ourselves if it’s just a layover city or if it’s worth a stop!

Our first stop was Baywalk, a very popular spot in Puerto Princesa, especially on weekends. It was buzzing with families enjoying the evening, with lots of food stalls and entertainment. We could see why it’s such a favourite hangout! We decided to sit at a restaurant for a drink, but things took a scary turn when a lorry crashed into the electric pole right outside, cutting the power and causing a bit of chaos. We cut our evening short but were ready early the next morning to continue exploring.

Next, we walked down to Plaza Quartel, a historical site where 150 American soldiers were imprisoned by the Japanese during World War II. Although it’s meant to be a peaceful park commemorating the fallen, it’s currently undergoing a 15 million peso rehabilitation programme, so there wasn’t much to see, and the area was mostly under construction. Nonetheless, it was still nice to visit and pay our respects.

With the rain starting to pour, we sought shelter back at our hotel while we waited for our 6-hour minivan journey up to El Nido.

description:
We set ourselves the task of ONLY eating street food for 24 hours whilst in Manila, for the simple reason that we fancied a challenge. We didn't realise it would open our minds (and taste buds!) up to a selection of new things and some of the tastiest food we've eaten in the Philippines so far. Many tourists or foreigners are wary about street food and it's associations with food poisoning or bad hygiene so we are here to debunk that! You are just as likely to get food poisoning from eating food in a restaurant and by avoiding street food, you're missing out on a wealth of different foods, tastes and very budget friendly options. 

Anyway, we started the day at Salcedo morning market (we filmed a whole video on this market and everything we ate there so go and check that video out too!) which had an amazing selection of both Filipino and International foods. We really enjoyed the weekend vibe and tried Hungarian sausage, empanadas, the Filipino food favourite chorizo pudpud and fresh juices.

description:
The weekend is here, which means we finally get to visit the Salcedo Morning Market. This famous market in Manila is a vibrant weekend destination offering a wide variety of fresh produce, local delicacies, organic goods, and handmade crafts. Located in Salcedo Village, Makati, it attracts locals and tourists alike with its lively atmosphere and diverse selection of high-quality food and artisanal products. It is open every Saturday from 7:00 AM to 2:00 PM.

We first heard about this from watching Dale Phillips’ vlog in Manila and have always wanted to go, but our timings never matched up. We started off by taking a Grab to the area (it wasn’t far to walk, but we didn’t want to get too sweaty before breakfast). We explored the amazing market for around 15 minutes, building up an appetite and deciding what we wanted to eat. 

After looping through the whole market, Jason spotted one of his favorite coffee shops, Tim Hortons. We’ve only ever had one coffee from there, called French Vanilla. It’s simply the best, and you must try it if you ever pass one. We enjoyed a coffee there, then headed off to get some delicious Hungarian sausage—it was incredibly juicy and tasty.

Next, we tried some empanadas (savory pastries filled with meat, vegetables, or cheese, then deep-fried or baked). There is a stand that offers a really well-priced meal of chorizo silog, which Jason enjoyed while Erin got herself a refreshing cucumber juice. The food was really fresh. The prices were a little high, but that was to be expected for the area and the quality of what we were eating. If you're in Manila on a Saturday, we highly recommend this as both a meal and an experience.

title: Living On The Philippines Largest Rubbish Dump 🇵🇭 Children of the Dump
tags: philippines|philippines vlog|philippines charity|charity work philippines|charity philippines|childrens charity|give back|fundraising|help the children|children of the dump|british couple visit philippines charity|charity in the philippines|donate now|make a difference|charity work|manila charity|philippines travel|philippines travel vlog|filipino vlogger|vlogger in the philippines|british couple vlog|british couple vlog philippines|charity|charity video
description:
We visited a children's charity in Manila, Children of the Dump, part of the Asian Student Christian Trust. This charity supports children and families who are living and working on Manila’s largest rubbish dump, a place where nobody should have to live. These families are living in incredibly difficult conditions and the children are fighting hard to have an education. This would be  impossible without the support of the Asian Student Christian Trust so we have made this video to help raise awareness and show the incredible work being done to give these children a chance at a better life.

💔 Philippines… these children need our help!

We visited the rubbish dump to see the heartbreaking situation for ourselves. Families are living alongside flies, rats and rubbish in a smelly and unclean environment. They live here because the parents work as scavengers, collecting plastic and metal from the rubbish dump and selling it to junk shops for a very small wage. Their houses are made from any materials they can scavenge and in some houses, there are 6 people sharing one bed. They do not have access to electricity or running water. Sometimes, children will help their parents scavenge on the rubbish dump instead of attending school because surviving has to come first. Their living situation is heartbreaking but we are determined to help. 

🤝 The Charity 

The charity ‘Children of the Dump’, part of the Asian Student Christian Trust, supports these families in many different ways. They run a free school which is located at the rubbish dump, which avoids any transport costs and means the children are put into education at a very early age. They also run free classes at the charity centre for over 140 children in the wider community, allowing them to further their education outside of public school, teaching a wide variety of classes from leadership, teamwork and dance. Of course these classes are not free to run and are solely reliant on donations from the public. 

The charity also provides a monthly supplement to some of the families living on the dump, helping with food and transport costs. The work this charity does is quite simply life changing. It’s a tough reality, but we want to shed light on the incredible work being done to help these children and provide them with a better future. The charity staff are so passionate about the work they do and are kind, caring and supportive people. In this video, we asked some of the staff to explain the work that the charity does and how it actually helps the community so you can hear it firsthand.

title: Where To Start a Backpacking Trip In South East Asia?
tags: Backpacking|Backpacker|Thailand|Malaysia|Langkawi|Travel|Travel vlog|Travel advice|Travel videos|Backpacking advice|South east Asia|South east Asia travel vlog
description:
So you’ve made the decision to backpack around south east Asia, but the next question is, where do you start?
People for many years have started their backpacking trips in Bangkok. More specifically Ko Sann Road. This is a fantastic place for any backpacker to start and has it all. But just because people for years have started there doesn’t mean you have to.

Langkawi, an archipelago of 99 islands off the coast of Malaysia, is a tropical paradise that offers backpackers a perfect blend of adventure, nature, and relaxation. Known for its stunning beaches, lush rainforests, and vibrant nightlife, Langkawi is an ideal destination for those looking to unwind or explore.
For beach lovers, Pantai Cenang is the main hub, with its lively atmosphere, budget accommodations, and array of bars and restaurants. If you prefer something quieter, head to the more tranquil beaches like Tanjung Rhu or Pantai Tengah. Nature enthusiasts will appreciate Langkawi’s UNESCO Global Geopark, where you can hike through rainforests, visit stunning waterfalls like Telaga Tujuh, and explore the mangroves by kayak or boat.

A must-do is the Langkawi Sky Bridge, an impressive curved suspension bridge offering breathtaking views of the surrounding islands. You can also take the cable car to the top of Gunung Mat Cincang for panoramic vistas of the island and its surrounding waters. For a bit of wildlife, the Langkawi Wildlife Park and Underwater World offer encounters with exotic creatures.
Despite its growing popularity, Langkawi still maintains a laid-back vibe that’s perfect for backpackers on a budget. Affordable hostels, guesthouses, and street food stalls abound, making it easy to keep costs low while enjoying all that the island has to offer. Whether you’re seeking adventure or simply a place to relax, Langkawi provides the perfect escape.

title: WE DID IT!! We drove our motorbikes from Hanoi to Ho Chi Minh and now the adventure is over 😢
tags: Vietnam|vietnam motorbike vlog|vietnam motorbike|places to ride motorbikes in Vietnam|top gear|top gear route Vietnam|Jeremy Clarkson|James may|the top gear route on motorbikes|travel|travel vlog|travel videos Vietnam|backpacking Vietnam|backpacker vlog|backpacking vietnam|things to do in Vietnam|south east Asia|south east asia travel vlog|moto vlog|motorbike vlog|motorbike trips|beautiful motorbike roads|motorbike vietnam|moto|vlog|travelling|travelvlog
description:
Motorbiking Vietnam for the last 2 months has been beautiful, scary, painful and so worth it. 

As we leave Mui Ne in the direction of our last stop, we both individually reflect on what the journey has meant to us. We give our motorbikes a good clean at our accommodation so they’re ready for the last ride and to be sold when we arrive in Ho Chi Minh City. 

The road leading to Ho Chi Minh was mundane, grey and BUSY. It felt like the whole of Vietnam were filtering their way towards the city on the same day as us.

Every kilometre close we got, it got 5% busier. It was so important to stay switched on so we didn’t fall (quite literally) at the last hurdle. 

The sky ahead was grey, like REALLY dark. A storm was brewing and we had 50km to go. As the rain started to splash on our helmets, we knew we were in trouble. We had never experienced rain quite like it. It was aggressive rain, the roads became flooded in ankle deep water within 30 minutes. We had to make a very quick decision to carry on or pull over and we chose to carry on, we were nearly there (we know 50km isn’t close but when we were looking at it from a “let’s finish this 2200km journey” it felt pretty close) 

Most motorbike drivers had pulled over taking shelter under bridges , lorries were whizzing past us and splashing us heavily as they did so. It was intense. Our camera equipment stopped working and our phones were barely hanging on… but eventually we made it to the comfort of Meander Hotel Saigon. 

With the entire contents of our backpacks completely soaked, it wasn’t the end we had in our mind but it was our end and we loved every minute of it. 

This was the last episode of our motorcycle diaries through Vietnam. We hope we have managed to entertain, educate or even inspire you. 

Thank you for watching, our trip in Vietnam has come to an end but we continue our journey on and we hope you are along for the ride too.

Erin & Jason

description:
We’ve been in Vietnam for almost 3 months and we have finally reached the sandy dunes of Mui Ne! 
Mui Ne is located on the south coast of Vietnam, around 200km away from Ho Chi Minh, but when you get there you would think you were thousands of miles away in the Sahara! 

The sand dunes here are not only beautiful but FUN! We booked to go on a jeep tour to see them (even though we have motorbikes, we like to have our rest days). The colourful jeep tours can be booked anywhere BUT we booked ours through our hotel “MAY BUNGALOW” (we would highly recommend staying here too if you fancy some affordable luxury).

The Jeep picked us up at 1.30pm for a couple of other touristy things such as the fairy stream & fishing village before heading off to the dunes. When we arrived at the white sand dunes we were greeted by some friendly Quad-bike drivers who have the set price of:

Option 1 
300,000 VND per person ($12) for a fun drive up to the sand dunes, over to the lake and back to the entrance. You get to stay at each place for as long as you want. 
Option 2 
800,000VND ($32) for 1 Quad-bike that you get to drive yourself BUT you have to be back at the entrance within 20 minutes. 

We thought about this for a few minutes before going for option 1 and we’re very glad we did as we got to spend more time at each place. 

Mui Ne is a cool town with nice bars, restaurants and things to do. You should definitely consider adding it to your itinerary either before or after Ho Chi Minh (depending on which way you’re travelling!). We stayed for 4 nights but if you’re tight on time, 2 nights could also work well.

title: The COOLEST Mountain Pass in Vietnam! #vietnam #travel #moto #motovlog #motorcycle #ngoanmucpass
tags: Vietnam|vietnam motorbike vlog|vietnam motorbike|places to ride motorbikes in Vietnam|top gear|top gear route Vietnam|Jeremy Clarkson|James may|the top gear route on motorbikes|travel|travel vlog|travel videos Vietnam|backpacking Vietnam|backpacker vlog|backpacking vietnam|things to do in Vietnam|south east Asia|south east asia travel vlog|moto vlog|motorbike vlog|motorbike trips|beautiful motorbike roads|motorbike vietnam|moto|vlog|travelling|travelvlog
description:
In this episode of our Vietnam motorbike diaries, we are leaving the cool climate of Da Lat and heading for the sunny coast - Mui Ne! We first drove from Da Lat to Mui Dinh (30km south of Phan Rang). As Da Lat is 1500km above sea level, we knew we were in for some steep slopes and a pretty sharp decline. This included driving on the Ngoạn Mục Pass (also known as the Sông Pha pass) which is the steepest mountain pass in southern Vietnam. 

The pass is 18.5km long at a 9 degree slope with many, many, MANY bends! Luckily, it was a beautiful sunny day so we could fly the drone and see some of the bends from the sky. The pass is also well known for Vietnam’s first hydroelectric power station situated at the bottom. During the pass, you get to drive directly underneath the two huge hydraulic water pipes that run over the mountain. 

After a descent of 700m, we made it to the bottom and could admire the enormous mountain we had just driven down and the sheer scale of the water pipes. We then stopped for some roadside pho before continuing on to Mui Dinh. Although there wasn’t much to do in Mui Dinh, we had heard about a beach front hotel providing a beach wave soundtrack throughout the night, and we really wanted to stay there. The hotel itself was quite basic but the location was incomparable and for £9 a night, a relaxing evening listening to the waves crash against the sand was just what we needed after a 140km drive. We also learned that we had narrowly escaped a flash food and landslide in Da Lat by a matter of hours and felt like the bad weather really is chasing us.

The next morning, after a ca phe sua da (Vietnamese iced coffee with condensed milk), we made our way to Mui Ne. Back on the QL1, we were driving against a Wild West looking backdrop of dusty mountains but with not much else to focus on. The drive was fairly mundane until we were about 30km outside of Mui Ne and the views were AMAZING! Sand dunes and wind turbines on our right, the sea on our left. We were driving in at about 2pm which is when the sunset tours leave from Mui Ne to the sand dunes and the brightly coloured jeeps speeding down the road provided some entertainment for us. 

We then checked into our accommodation, a wonderful hotel with a massive pool called May Bungalow, and headed down to Pineapple Beach Bar where we enjoyed a beer or two and watched 20 or so fishermen casting their nets in front of a beautiful sunset. 

This is our second last biking vlog of the series, next up Ho Chi Minh City! Thank you for watching and please remember to like and subscribe if you enjoyed the video.

E&J :)

description:
In this travel vlog, we explore the quirky mountain town of Da Lat in Vietnam, a place with over 1,000 hotels but not much to do—at least, that’s what we thought! After a long motorbike ride through the bustling streets of Vietnam, we finally arrived in Da Lat, expecting a serene escape into the mountains. 

However, what we found was a town with a strange abundance of hotels, most of which seemed almost empty or had just a few rooms occupied. It left us scratching our heads—why are there so many hotels in a town that feels relatively quiet and less touristy than other spots in Vietnam?

Located 1,500 meters above sea level, Da Lat offers a cooler climate compared to the rest of Vietnam, making it a popular retreat from the heat of the lowlands. The temperature is much cooler, often requiring only a light jacket, and the town doesn't even need air conditioning or fans in most hotels. 

The cool climate and stunning mountainous landscapes make it an ideal spot for locals seeking a weekend getaway and for a few international travelers looking to enjoy some peace and tranquility. Da Lat is also known for its French colonial architecture, charming cafes, and scenic views of lakes and forests, which provide a peaceful atmosphere perfect for unwinding.

Despite the town’s low-key vibe, Da Lat still manages to have some fun attractions. We decided to check out the alpine coaster, one of the town's main highlights. The coaster takes you on a thrilling 20-minute ride down the mountainside to Datanla Waterfall, one of the area's most famous natural sights. It was an exciting experience, and we couldn’t resist buying a ride photo as a memento of the adventure! It costs 250,000 VND each (£7.70) but we got sucked into buying the ride photo at a cost of 90,000 VND (£2.70) as well. 

After the ride, we stopped by Goc Ha Thanh, a local restaurant, to try wonton soup—our first time tasting this delicious dish, and it certainly didn’t disappoint. Of course, we also got caught in the rain while wandering around, but it didn’t stop us from exploring the area.

As we spent more time in Da Lat, we couldn’t help but wonder why there are so many hotels in a place that seems so quiet and peaceful, with fewer attractions than other tourist-heavy areas in Vietnam. If you have any theories or insights, please leave us a comment below! We’d love to hear your thoughts on this mysterious phenomenon.

description:
Buying our own motorbikes in Hanoi and riding all the way down to Ho Chi Minh City has given us the freedom to explore off-the-beaten-path destinations in Vietnam. After leaving Hoi An, we made our way to My Son Sanctuary, a UNESCO World Heritage site in central Vietnam, home to ancient Hindu temples built by the Champa Kingdom between the 4th and 13th centuries. The site offers rich history, stunning architecture, and breathtaking scenery. Though many of the temples were destroyed in the war, we enjoyed exploring the site and could have spent much more time there if we didn’t have 110km to cover.

Arriving in Kham Duc, we rested before starting our day with an incredibly cheap iced coffee. Kham Duc is a small town in central Vietnam, located along the historic Ho Chi Minh Road. Surrounded by lush mountains and dense forests, it offers a peaceful escape with traditional food, waterfalls, and local culture. During the Vietnam War, Kham Duc was strategically important, with the U.S. establishing a military base here. Today, it remains a quiet, off-the-beaten-path destination, where travelers can learn about its history, enjoy rural landscapes, and experience local life. Its relaxed atmosphere and proximity to the Vietnam War history make it a unique stop on any journey through central Vietnam.

Jason spotted a nearby waterfall on his map, and with the help of two friendly local boys, we found it! Our Vietnamese isn’t great, but we managed to eat a delicious chicken noodle soup with peanuts and mild chili sauce—simple, but tasty. 

We also joined a local yoga class at our homestay and later indulged in beef noodles and Bánh xèo (Vietnamese crispy pancake), both of which were incredible. Bánh xèo (one of our favourite dishes) s a Vietnamese crispy pancake made from rice flour, turmeric, and coconut milk. It’s typically filled with shrimp, pork, bean sprouts, and herbs, then folded and served with fresh greens and a tangy dipping sauce. A delicious street food! The food, the culture, and the people of Kham Duc made it the perfect stop on our journey along the Ho Chi Minh road.

description:
We arrived at our hotel in Plei Kan and wanted to visit the Indochina T Junction whilst staying the night in Plei Kan. The Indochina T Junction is where Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia all share a border and there is a monument symbolising their friendship that you can visit. However, after putting the wrong location into our offline maps, we ended up at the Laos-Vietnam border instead. We had absolutely no idea that as we approached and the immigration officer waved us through, we had actually left Vietnam. 

We drove round ‘no man’s land’ for a while, even buying a soft drink from a Laos shop, until we reached the entrance of Laos and the guard told us to stop and asked for our passports. We quickly realised our mistake and drove back to the entrance into Vietnam. However, this is where things took a turn for the worse...

The guard who initially waved us through the Vietnam gate came over and was shouting at us, saying that he told us to stop and demanding to see our passports. This did not happen but unfortunately we didn’t catch it on camera so cannot prove anything (other than the fact no one shouted after us or came after us on bikes once we had gone through the gate). We were denied entrance into Vietnam for about 5 minutes and could not easily explain our mistake due to a huge language barrier. 

Eventually, there was no other option but for them to let us through as we could not communicate and we think it was pretty obvious we hadn’t entered Laos as we were only 5 minutes and had one small bag with us. The whole experience was quite scary and after reading reviews of the border crossing online, we realise how lucky we were to get back through without having to pay anything! 

If you want to see what happened, we made a longer video over on our channel! To be kept up to date with our journey please like, subscribe and turn on your video notifications.

description:
Motorbiking Through Vietnam’s Ho Chi Minh Road: Lo Xo Pass, Indochina Junction, & Unexpected Border Crossing!

🌍 Join us as we journey from Hoi An to Kham Duc, Plei Kan, Pleiku, and beyond, exploring the stunning countryside, rural Vietnam, and experiencing unexpected challenges, all while learning about the culture and history along the way.

🚴‍♀️ What is it REALLY like to motorbike through Vietnam’s rugged backroads? We travel off-the-beaten-path, from the Lo Xo Pass to the serene Sea Lake near Pleiku, sharing the highs and lows of the ride.

Leaving Hoi An felt chaotic. We hadn’t been on the bikes for a while, so we were a bit rusty. The traffic was dense, and it took a while to get used to the flow again. Once we hit the quieter roads, it was a relief, and the ride became much smoother. Our destination that day was Kham Duc, 111km west of Hoi An.

We made a quick detour to My Son Sanctuary, a collection of Hindu temples built between the 4th and 13th centuries by the Champa kings. The site, though partially in ruins, was still a fascinating glimpse into Vietnam’s ancient past. We’ve got a full video about My Son on our channel – be sure to check it out!

After exploring the temples, we were back on the road toward Kham Duc. The rain started pouring again, and the ride became even tougher. Our bodies were not used to long rides, so every bump on the road felt brutal! But as we drove deeper into rural Vietnam, the landscape grew more beautiful, and the sight of smiling locals made the struggle worth it.

We arrived in Kham Duc and checked into the cozy 21 Guesthouse and Yoga. The owner was incredibly friendly and gave us great tips for local food and things to do. After drying off our clothes, we indulged in a warm meal of Bánh xèo and hit the hay for a much-needed rest.

The next morning, we were off to Plei Kan, 110km away. We were excited to see the Lo Xo Pass – though we didn’t quite know what to expect! We left the guesthouse, only for Erin to discover she had a flat tire. Fortunately, a mechanic nearby fixed it for just 30,000 VND (about £1).

As we continued, the roads became a challenge. For two hours, we encountered cracked concrete roads, roadworks, and aggressive trucks honking and driving too close. We had to stay alert the entire time, which meant we didn’t get a chance to enjoy the Lo Xo Pass – and only realized we’d passed through it much later!

We arrived in Plei Kan around 2pm, dropped our bags at the hotel, and set out again to see the Indochina Junction, a monument where the borders of Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos meet. But things took a wild turn when we accidentally crossed into Laos! We had trouble getting back into Vietnam, and it became quite an ordeal. We’ve made a separate video about this crazy experience – stay tuned for that!

Next, we visited the famous Sea Lake (Bien Ho), a large freshwater lake near Pleiku. It’s known for its “sea-like” waves during the rainy season, making it a must-see. Since we were in coffee plantation territory, we decided to visit a local coffee farm. Erin had found one with an adjoining café, so we took a Grab taxi. However, the driver abandoned us halfway down a dirt track because the road was so bad. The café was closed, and we were stranded with no Wi-Fi. 

We hiked back to the nearest town and managed to call a taxi back to Pleiku. Exhausted and frustrated, we grabbed some pizza and crashed for the night, ready for the next day’s adventure.

This is the 7th episode of our motorbiking journey through Vietnam. We hope to make it safely to Ho Chi Minh City while experiencing as much of the country as possible and documenting it for our future selves and all of you watching!

Thank you for watching! If you enjoyed this video, please remember to like this video and subscribe to our channel :)

title: The Hai Van Pass By Motorcycle #motovlog #motorcycle #vietnam #travel  #vietnamtravelguide
tags: Vietnam|vietnam motorbike vlog|vietnam motorbike|places to ride motorbikes in Vietnam|the hai van pass|top gear|top gear route Vietnam|Jeremy Clarkson|James may|Richard hammond|the top gear route on motorbikes|travel|travel vlog|travel videos Vietnam|backpacking Vietnam|backpacker vlog|backpacking vietnam|things to do in Vietnam|south east Asia|south east asia travel vlog|hai van pass|moto vlog|motorbike vlog|motorbike trips|beautiful motorbike roads
description:
The Hai Van Pass, one of the most famous and beautiful roads to motorbike in Vietnam. This is the route we will be taking on this episode BUT we have a little bit to go before we get to it. We leave the bustling ancient city of Hue and head directly east. 

We found a lovely coastal route in our Lonely Planet book (south east Asia on a shoestring). This route is called “Tombs & Dunes” and it’s only around 15km away from Hue. It was a different ride and beautiful in its own way as we followed the coastline with the sea to our left. We stayed the night nearby at a place called Villa Louise/Hue Beach Bar. We recommend staying here if you have the time on your trip as it’s only 25 minutes away from Hue and it has a beautiful private beach. 

The next morning we set off in the direction of Da Nang via the coastline. The ride itself was beautiful, especially towards the end (15km before joining Highway 1) as we passed through some lovely winding roads next to where the river meets the sea. 

The stretch of road on the QL1 was nothing to phone home about. Just big old lorries and buses who always drive as if they’re late to the airport. 

However the Hai Van Pass was approaching, the increased sign of backpackers on motorbikes and easy riders was getting more and more. It’s not incredibly sign posted though, just as you approach the turning for it we saw the first sign for it. You can’t actually drive underneath the Hai Van pass as motorbikes are not allowed in the tunnel. 

It’s so exciting finally seeing the sign for it, we’ve grown up watching Top Gear specials including the famous Vietnam one. this is where we first ever heard about this route and I’m sure a lot of people can say the same. Watching Jeremy Clarkson, James May & Richard Hammond take this journey has inspired many other tourists to take this road. 

It was a happy accident when we started riding as the train was going alongside the road, clinking its way on the tracks was really picturesque. The ascent was so beautiful; the view of the sea, the curves of the road and the sun shining could only bring smiles to our faces. Seeing the famous twists and turns from the drone really gave us a feel for the roads we were driving on. 

We stopped at the top of the Hai Van Pass to take in the view, drink some coffee and visit the Hai Van Gate/ fortress that was last used by the Americans during the war. Lucky for us this only became free in August 2024, so great timing to save a couple of dollars! 

We decided to head down after our short break. We got back on the bikes and headed towards Da Nang. Jason’s tyre was almost completely flat as we rode off, he was told that there was someone about 2KM down that would be able to help (we recommend you watch the video to see/hear the funny story of what took place during this time).

The Hai Van Pass was now complete… just in time for the rains to begin. Ponchos on, we rode into Da Nang city, the roads were really bad. They were full of huge puddles in the bike lane and heavy traffic. It’s the worst traffic we’ve experienced so far on our drive and that’s saying something as we left from Hanoi. Thousands of bikes and cars all weaving and beeping their way through rush our traffic. Jason had a car drive into the back of him (slowly but still a collision) and Erin the same as she had to place her feet down to stop a fall. 

Finally at the hostel (Backpacker Hostel & spa) we took a deep exhale at the juxtaposition of what had just happened, beauty and then the beast. BUT as we thought we were safe things got worse. Erin was filming herself for this video (taking her bags off the bike and debriefing) and out of nowhere a HUGE clash of lightning happened just above our heads. So close that the staff in the hostel that witnessed it, shouted at us to come inside. We had no idea what it was. It scared us so much, just as the adrenaline wore off from the ride it was pushed back into our bodies again as we scrambled to get the bags in, an eventful end to an eventful ride.


This is the 6th episode of our motorbiking journey through the wonderful country of Vietnam and we not only hope to arrive safely in Ho Chi Minh but to experience this beautiful country as much possible and to document it for anyone watching (including our future selves).

If you would like to be kept up to date with our journey please like, subscribe and turn on your video notifications. 

Thank you so much

We have arrived in Hue, located in central Vietnam with a population of 650,000… plus 2 hungry Brits! We have a small itinerary; the abandoned waterpark, the Imperial Citadel and of course, to EAT! 

Due to the central location of this ancient city, it not only has its own famous dishes  BUT it pulls in flavours from both north and south Vietnam, creating this AMAZING melting pot of food & exciting menus for us to read. 

We start this foodie vlog by trying the infamous ‘DMZ BAR’. Fun fact about this place, it was the first pub to open up in Hue after the war ended. It began trading in 1994 & has just celebrated its 30th birthday! 

Trying a tasty platter of local foods; lemongrass pork stuffed into rice paper, fresh spring rolls & Hue crispy pancake (filled with pork & egg). This bar is a really good starting point for anyone visiting Hue for the first time. It has a good mix of local and western food with lovely staff & and a great atmosphere. 

We then picked up the best fresh juice we’ve had on our trip so far. The lady added no sugar to our drinks so what we saw was exactly what we got. Tasty, fresh, super cheap iced juice. We don’t have a name for this stand but it was directly opposite the ‘Win Mart’ store on Nguyen Cong Tru street :) 

Our next meal was at Hue’s bustling Dong Ba market. In search of “parts unknown” or in other words Anthony Bourdain’s Bun Bo Hue Lady. This place was featured on the late great Anthony Bourdain programme, in the particular episode he ate what he later described as “the best soup he’s ever eaten in his life” SOLD. After walking around trying to find this stall, we had to ask a security guard for help, he smiled and showed us the way. 

The lady welcomed us with open arms and a smiling face. The soup was SO cheap and extremely tasty. The portions weren’t massive but she also sold skewers, which again, were cheap and tasty. We’d highly recommend going there and sitting in the place where the legend himself sat so his and her legend may continue in the thing that brings us all together… food. 

The next day we tried out Ba Tam. This restaurant is part of the Nook group in Hue. They have 3 restaurants in the area Ba Tam, Mingle vegetarian cafe & the Nook Eatery. We found out about this place whilst eating at The Nook (if you’re wondering why that wasn’t in the video, they had a power cut after we placed our order. It was too dark to film BUT, somehow the food came out. It’s a great place if you fancy a western style breakfast or brunch). Ba Tam offers a more traditional side to Hue’s food, with their ethos being more local home comfort food & eating tasty dishes that lots of people grew up eating in the area. It was really good. 

Our last meal was a small street food restaurant with pumping music & tables of smoking locals called ‘Dac San’. We decided to try a few things we hadn’t eaten before including spicy steamed clams & fried frogs in fish sauce. Both extremely good and in all honesty, two things we’d like to eat again.

title: Riding from Khe Sanh to Hue in Typhoon Winds – Vietnam Motorbike Route
tags: Moto vlog|Motorcycle|Motorbike vlogs|Motorbike Vietnam vlog|Motorcycle Vietnam videos|Motorbike Vietnam vloggers|Travel videos Vietnam|Travel Vietnam by motorcycle|Tourists on motorbike Vietnam|Is Vietnam safe for tourists|Hue Vietnam|Vietnam travel videos|Backpackers in Vietnam|backpacking Vietnam vlog|Vietnam travel itinerary|Vietnam number 1|Motorcycle vlog|Vietnam travel vlog|Hue travel itinerary|Things to see in Hue
description:
Our 2-month journey through Vietnam continues with a massive 1600km ride, all the way from Hanoi to Hue, on two motorbikes we bought in Hanoi. After two successful days riding along the iconic Ho Chi Minh Highway, we arrived in Khe Sanh—a stopover on our journey that didn’t hold much for us apart from the Khe Sanh Museum. We only stayed one night before setting our sights on Hue.

Before leaving, we took a break in a local coffee shop, discussing our route for the day as a typhoon was heading toward the north. We could already feel the effects of the strong winds in Khe Sanh, and we knew it was important to plan our route carefully for safety.

With coffee in hand and water bottles fueling us up, we headed south toward Dong Ha. But just 5 minutes into our ride, Erin noticed a flat tyre, so we stopped by a friendly local mechanic for a quick fix. With the wind picking up and light rain falling, the ride to Dong Ha was a bit challenging, and we missed the calmness of the Ho Chi Minh Trail.

We arrived in Dong Ha around 1pm and treated ourselves to a little comfort at the Saigon Hotel, costing just £10 each for a spacious and luxurious room. After checking in, we quickly booked a taxi to the Vinh Moc Tunnels—a decision we were glad we made as the wind was even stronger. The taxi ride was £18 for a return trip, a small price to pay for comfort after a rough couple of days.

If you want to learn more about the Vinh Moc Tunnels, make sure to check out our Hue Vlog for the full experience.

The next morning, after the winds calmed slightly, we set off for Hue on our motorbikes. Along the way, we were passed by 20-25 green army trucks, likely returning from supporting Hanoi during Typhoon Yagi.

We arrived in Hue at around 2pm, and immediately felt the pulse of the city. Traffic in Hue was hectic, especially around the bridges, but our backpacks tied to our bikes gave the locals an indication that we were new to the area, and they gave us the space we needed.

While this ride wasn’t as scenic as our time on the Ho Chi Minh Trail, it led us toward more incredible roads, including the legendary Hai Van Pass, which will be the highlight of our next adventure. Stay tuned for more as we continue our journey through Vietnam on motorbikes! 🏍️

This is the 5th episode of our motorbiking journey through the wonderful country of Vietnam and we not only hope to arrive safely in Ho Chi Minh but to experience this beautiful country as much possible and to document it for anyone watching (including our future selves).

Thank you for watching! If you enjoyed this video, please remember to like this video and subscribe to our channel :)

We motorbiked from Khe Sanh to Dong Ha specifically to visit the Vinh Moc tunnels in the DMZ, right on the border of North and South Vietnam. We decided to get a taxi there as we were experiencing the tail end of Typhoon Yagi and it was very windy. We were so surprised by how narrow the tunnels were and could not comprehend that approximately 60 families lived in these tunnels during the war; mothers gave birth, children played, and they all sheltered from the bombs raining down on them. The tunnels stretch for about 2km so we explored as much as we could, descending 20m deep to the lowest floor. The tunnels aren't well lit so it got quite difficult to find our way through in the pitch black, but if you just keep walking, you soon find your way out of one of the entrances (usually walking right out onto the huge white stretch of sand). 

The next day, we motorbiked down to Hue where we visited the abandoned waterpark, Hồ Thủy Tiên, about 10km away from Hue. We had to pay 20,000 VND each to enter (Vietnamese locals said it was a cleaning fee) and 10,000 VND to park our motorbike. The lake surrounding the iconic dragon statue has completely dried up now and there was lots of construction going on in the area so it didn't really feel abandoned at all, aside from the graffti covering the buildings, the smashed glass in the old aquarium and the fact that there was only about 5 other people there. We weren't allowed to drive our motorbike around the waterpark as planned and due to the ongoing construction works, we couldn't get to the abandoned slides or theatre either. It was cool to see and explore the dragon building but it wasn't quite what we expected. 

We then visited the Imperial City, the ancient capital of unified Vietnam. It cost 200,000 VND each to enter but this was so worth it to see all the beautiful buildings. We also paid 100,000 VND for a VR (virtual reality) experience where you fly over the ancient city and can see all of the buildings from above. This was fun and we also appreciated the air conditioning in the room!

description:
We left Phong Nha after staying there for 15 DAYS!! (we originally only intended on staying there for 3 days, but we loved it that much we found it really hard to leave). If you’re including Phong Nha on your Vietnam itinerary, we recommend you add at least 2 days on top of your original plan… it’s great) 

Staying in Phong Nha longer gave us time to relax, visit paradise cave, have our motorbikes serviced, experience Vietnam national day and spend Jason’s birthday in a familiar place. 

We decided to get ourselves (and the motorbikes) off of the infamous QL1 better known as highway 1. If you haven’t driven down it before you’re not missing out on a great deal (in the north especially) it’s a mixture of loud lorries, fast moving buses on a mission & a huge headache.

The road we decided to take was the much more beautiful ‘Ho Chi Minh Trail’ road. This road is not only one of the most beautiful motorbikes drives in Vietnam, it runs really close the Laos border with its many swoops and bends.

The total drive from Phong Nha to Khe Sanh is 233Km which we did over the course of 2 days. The first 99Km drive was to Lon Son, a small town situated in between huge limestone hills/mountain like structures. 

It was a really hot day and we stupidly did not pack enough water, between us we had just over 1.5litres. We expected to see some roadside sellers along the way but after about 1 hour we realised this wasn’t going to happen. We only passed about 10 other people driving this day, which means the road itself isn’t busy enough to be able to warrant people selling food & drink on the roads like we’ve been used to seeing so far. 

We arrived in Lon son at 2.30pm (which made the total drive 4 hours) we had a few stops in between to allow the bikes to cool down and also take in some of the scenery around us. 

We found a place to stay (name of hotel unknown but it was the only place to stay in the area) it cost 300,000 VND / £9 / $12 for a basic but decent hotel room with air-con, hot shower & comfy bed (three things that feel amazing after a days ride).

Jason started his bike to get fuel, and realised his bikes electrics weren’t functioning properly. Luckily in this small town there was a mechanic right next to the hotel, a new battery was fitted & this was completed in 10 minutes costing 400,000 VND / £12 / $16. 

The hotel we stayed in cooked us some rice, vegetables and meat which went down really well alongside some Pringles, sweets & film in bed. 

The next day we set off at 9am, it rained heavily in the night and was lightly raining in the morning BUT this was as good as it was going to get. 
The rain didn’t stop, it was lightly raining for most of the drive (and some parts towards the end VERY heavily) a small incident occurred whilst driving, one of the bungee cords holding Jason’s bag in place suddenly snapped and got trapped in his wheel whilst driving, luckily nothing happened when it did but it could have been a lot worse.

We experienced so many friendly faces on this drive, every time we drove past someone (mainly children) we received either a wave or a huge “HELLOOOOO” and apart from some beautiful waterfalls on the side of the road and driving through thick clouds/fog at the top of a very high mountain where we couldn’t see 10 metres in front of us, not much happened on this drive. We tried to keep our heads down and make it to Khe Sanh safely, which we did at about 3pm. It took us quite a while to do this 134KM drive as the weather was awful and in Jason’s words “the hardest drive I’ve ever done in my life” (this was due to weather not by any means the beautiful scenery and roads) 

This is the 4 episode of our motorbiking journey through the wonderful country of Vietnam and we not only hope to arrive safely in Ho Chi Minh but to experience this beautiful country as much possible and to document it for anyone watching (including our future selves).

If you would like to be kept up to date with our journey please like, subscribe and turn on your video notifications. 

Thank you so much 
E&J

description:
We motorbiked from Khe Sanh to Dong Ha specifically to visit the Vinh Moc tunnels in the DMZ, right on the border of North and South Vietnam. We decided to get a taxi there as we were experiencing the tail end of Typhoon Yagi and it was very windy. We were so surprised by how narrow the tunnels were and could not comprehend that approximately 60 families lived in these tunnels during the war; mothers gave birth, children played, and they all sheltered from the bombs raining down on them. The tunnels stretch for about 2km so we explored as much as we could, descending 20m deep to the lowest floor. The tunnels aren't well lit so it got quite difficult to find our way through in the pitch black, but if you just keep walking, you soon find your way out of one of the entrances (usually walking right out onto the huge white stretch of sand). 

The next day, we motorbiked down to Hue where we visited the abandoned waterpark, Hồ Thủy Tiên, about 10km away from Hue. We had to pay 20,000 VND each to enter (Vietnamese locals said it was a cleaning fee) and 10,000 VND to park our motorbike. The lake surrounding the iconic dragon statue has completely dried up now and there was lots of construction going on in the area so it didn't really feel abandoned at all, aside from the graffti covering the buildings, the smashed glass in the old aquarium and the fact that there was only about 5 other people there. We weren't allowed to drive our motorbike around the waterpark as planned and due to the ongoing construction works, we couldn't get to the abandoned slides or theatre either. It was cool to see and explore the dragon building but it wasn't quite what we expected. 

We then visited the Imperial City, the ancient capital of unified Vietnam. It cost 200,000 VND each to enter but this was so worth it to see all the beautiful buildings. We also paid 100,000 VND for a VR (virtual reality) experience where you fly over the ancient city and can see all of the buildings from above. This was fun and we also appreciated the air conditioning in the room! 

Thank you for watching and if you got this far, please like this video and subscribe to our channel for more.

title: Duck Stop in Phong Nha Vietnam, WORTH IT! #phongnha #duckstop #backpacking #vietnamtravel
tags: Duck stop Vietnam|Duck stop|The duck stop|The duck stop Vietnam|The duck stop phong nha|Ducks|Funny duck videos|Travel|Travel videos Vietnam|Travel shorts|Things to do in Vietnam|Things to do in phong nha|Duck leader Vietnam|Funny animal videos|Backpacking Vietnam|the duck stop phong nha|vietnam vlog|things to do phong nha|phong nha travel itinerary|vietnam travel itinerary|must do in vietnam|what to do in phong nha|phong nha|backpacker vlog
description:
Whilst visiting Phong Nha, we HAD to visit The Duck Stop, one of the most popular tourist attractions in the area! This HILARIOUS attraction in Phong Nha is an absolute must do on your Vietnam itinerary and we can see why so many people travel to Phong Nha just to do this! 

We paid 100,000 dong each (approx £3) and this included one soft drink/beer, 20 minutes with the ducks and crispy pancakes, the best food we've had in Vietnam so far. And of course meeting the friendliest Vietnamese people who own the farm and learning all about the crops they grow there. We were absolutely in love with the ducks and had the best experience, we haven't laughed so hard in a long time. You get to feed them, become a 'duck leader', hold one and have a special duck massage which is a feeling that really cannot be explained.

We also learnt so much about Vietnamese culture and traditional farm life; growing rice, fruit trees and why they keep the different animals on the farm. One of these animals was Mr Donald Trump, a 10 year old 700 kilo rescue water buffalo, who you can meet for an extra 50,000 dong (approx £1.50). It was amazing to get so close to him and learn more about these beautiful giants that we see every single day in Vietnam.

At the end of the experience, we were served a traditional Vietnamese crispy pancake (Bánh xèo) wrapped in rice paper and homemade peanut sauce made on the farm. We were taught how to prepare it, eat it and it was SO delicious.

description:
We’ve now started our 2 month journey through Vietnam and a whopping 1600km ride, on 2 motorbikes that we have purchased. 

In this episode we travel 180km from the bustling high rise city Vinh to the adventure capital of Vietnam Phong Nha. It wasn’t the best ride coming out of Vinh, lots of traffic and not many working indicators. 

We left the main city and drove around 15km to visit the native home of President Ho Chi Minh, where is family home was located. The site was a lot busier than we expected with many visitors (mostly Vietnamese) we seem to attract a lot of attention with many people asking for selfies and saying “welcome to Vietnam” which was lovely, we don’t think a lot of western tourists visit here, or at least they didn’t on this day. 

We only stayed here for maybe 30 minutes as we had a long day of riding ahead of us in the strong midday heat/ we had to get back to our motorbikes because everything we possessed on this trip was currently tied to the back of them. 

We began our ride to the town of Ky Anh which we chose as it was the middle of our final destination Phong Nha. 
When we arrived in this town we found a cheap hotel (the only hotel available) packed our bags and almost fell straight to sleep. 

The next day we drove to Phong Nha, we got to experience some dangerous moments along the way like animals in the road and driving through tunnels with sunglasses on (please don’t do this). Afterwards we then got the beautiful moments and the famous Ho Chi Minh Trail, the more beautiful road to motorbike on in Vietnam than the infamous Highway 1.

We accidentally caught on camera where our money was handed to after giving it to the coffee shop owner but you will have to make up your own minds as to the reason why!

title: Short But Sweaty Walk Up To Viewpoint. #Travel #Vietnam #NinhBinh #TravelShorts
tags: Vietnam|Travel|Travel vlog|Travel vlog Vietnam|Vietnam travel|Beautiful Vietnam|Places to see in Vietnam|Things to do in Vietnam|How long should I spend in Vietnam|Backpacker in Vietnam vlog|Backpackers in Vietnam|South east Asia viewpoints|Is south east Asia a good place for solo travelers|South east Asia travel vlog|Mua cave|Mua caves in Vietnam|Ninh Binh|Ninh Binh travel vlog
description:
We spent 3 nights in Ninh Binh, Tam Coc to be precise. We arrived here from Hanoi after our first journey of around 100km on our long north to south of Vietnam motorbiking adventure. 
During our 3 night stay we decided to take our motorbikes out on a smaller adventure within an adventure, to the famous Mua Cave.
As we arrived at the entrance to the attraction we  had to pull the breaks pretty fast as a herd (We think that’s what you’d call it) of water buffalo stood in our way. We weren’t going to chance it so waited patiently for a good time to go.
We arrived at the site during the hottest part of the day and paid the 200,000 VND entrance fee ($4 per person). 
We took a walk around the lotus flower lake, which wasn’t in peak bloom but it was really stunning none the less. After flying our drone, we decided to head over to the cave to get out of the suns full glaze… and see the cave of course. 
We then headed up to the viewpoint which was a tougher climb than expected, it took around 20 relaxed minutes but it was really worth the view of Ninh Binhs Beautiful landscape. 
There is a little shop (a person with a fridge) near the top so don’t worry if you run out of fluid as they sell lots of tasty cans and water. 

We hope you enjoyed the video and if you want to see more from us please like, subscribe, comment and all of that usual jazz!

description:
We spent 3 nights in Ninh Binh, Tam Coc to be precise. We arrived here from Hanoi after our first journey of around 100km on our long north to south of Vietnam motorbiking adventure. 
During our 3 night stay we decided to take our motorbikes out on a smaller adventure within an adventure, to the famous Mua Cave.
As we arrived at the entrance to the attraction we  had to pull the breaks pretty fast as a herd (We think that’s what you’d call it) of water buffalo stood in our way. We weren’t going to chance it so waited patiently for a good time to go.
We arrived at the site during the hottest part of the day and paid the 200,000 VND entrance fee ($4 per person). 
We took a walk around the lotus flower lake, which wasn’t in peak bloom but it was really stunning none the less. After flying our drone, we decided to head over to the cave to get out of the suns full glaze… and see the cave of course. 
We then headed up to the viewpoint which was a tougher climb than expected, it took around 20 relaxed minutes but it was really worth the view of Ninh Binhs Beautiful landscape. 
There is a little shop (a person with a fridge) near the top so don’t worry if you run out of fluid as they sell lots of tasty cans and water. 

We hope you enjoyed the video and if you want to see more from us please like, subscribe, comment and all of that usual jazz!

description:
Ninh Binh was our first stop after leaving Hanoi and we stayed in Tam Coc for 2 days to really soak up all the scenic beauty (it is a UNESCO World Heritage site after all!). Tam Coc means "Three Caves" so we set off on a boat trip to pass through them all - Ca, Hai and Ba. This trip cost 350,000 dong per person (£10) and took about 3 hours, rowing 3km down the river on a wooden boat, passing beautiful limestone structures and rice paddies. You can see why this place is locally known as "Ha Long Bay on land". A detail unique to Tam Coc is that the people rowing the boats (mostly women) use their feet to row the paddles instead of their hands and with such skill, it's amazing to watch. Once off the boat, we took an electric car to visit some temples dotted around the tranquil village, most notably the Thai Vi Temple and Bich Dong Pagoda where we flew our drone to capture the emerland green lagoon surrounding the bridge.

description:
We’ve now started our 2 month journey through Vietnam and a whopping 1600km ride, on 2 motorbikes that we have purchased. 

After buying the motorbikes in Hanoi and getting them/us set up for the trip (and waiting for the unpredictable Vietnamese rain to stop) we headed off on our first days ride to the town of Tam Coc in Ninh Binh. This ride should have taken us roughly 2-3 hours but we always knew it would take longer due to getting used to the bikes, traffic and most of all the before mentioned Vietnamese rain! 

It was a clear ride for the first part but we soon had to stop after about 1 hour of motorbiking to put our rain ponchos on (little did we know this would be done 3 times). The ride itself was fairly simple as we stuck to highway 1 with only one turn off 10km away from Ninh Binh to take us to Tam Coc. 

This is the first episode of our motorbiking journey through the wonderful country of Vietnam and we not only hope to arrive safely in Ho Chi Minh but to experience this beautiful country as much possible and to document it for anyone watching (including our future selves).

If you would like to be kept up to date with our journey please like, subscribe and turn on your video notifications.

description:
We’re about to start moving south of Hanoi in Vietnam and this time we’re not taking the usual mode of transportation. We’ve spent the last 10 months in south east Asia moving from place to place via every mode of transport possible. Sleeper buses in Laos, sleeper ferries in the Philippines, jam packed mini vans in Cambodia  and flights in Thailand. You name it, we’ve done it! We’re now taking the transport into our own hands by purchasing a couple of motorbikes. It’s a scary route to take in Vietnam and not for the faint of heart.

In this Hanoi travel vlog we stock up on the essentials needed for biking through Vietnam and staying safe on the roads during rainy season. 

The first item we purchase is a Vietnamese flag, this is more for aesthetic reasons/hoping local Vietnamese drivers see us with it and “take it easy on us”.

The second item we purchased (after a bit of haggling in Hanoi) was 2 thick rain ponchos, the ponchos even go over the motorbikes  themselves… and keep us dry too of course!

We then headed to get some new motorbike helmets, we decided to go for brand new helmets as we wanted to make sure they had never been in a previous accident before, in turn damaging their structure. We bought the motorcycle helmets from…
Cong Ty Tnhn Nhua Huyen Anh 
In the old quarter of Hanoi at the fixed price of 1.7 Million VND ($68). 

With a successful day so far of shopping in Hanoi, we headed to the famous indoor market “Dong Xuan Market” to see if we could find a reasonably priced motorbike phone holder. 

Last on the list was a metal bracket extension (thing) for Jason’s motorbike, his bike doesn’t have the same structure as Erin’s so had to have one handmade on a metal and welding street he found in Hanoi’s old quarter. 

If you’re still reading this, please like this video and subscribe to our channel for more.

title: (6/6) Trying To Find The Man In The Photo #hanoi #vietnam #reunion #vietnamvlog #travelvlog #travel
tags: Hanoi travel vlog|Emotional family reunion|Emotional story in Vietnam|Finding an old friend video|Vietnam travel|Backpacking in Vietnam|Is Vietnam good for backpackers?|Vietnam travel Vlog|British backpacker in Vietnam|Is Hanoi a safe place to visit?|How long to spend in Vietnam?|Vietnam travel itinerary|Things to do in Hanoi|Places to visit in Hanoi|Hanoi Vietnam travel Vlog|reunion|reunited|family reunion|family reunited|long lost family|long lost families
description:
10 years ago in 2014, I (a 20 year old Jason) was travelling through Vietnam, more specifically to this story Hanoi. 

One night, I was sat on a tiny stool in a street bar next to a busy road filled with only locals. I got chatting to this table of older Vietnamese men, who then invited us (me and my new friends Fraser and Orla) to sit with them. I don’t remember much of what we talked about with those men, but I do remember it being wholesome. 

Before we parted ways one of the men (Tao was his name) gave me an old photograph of his younger self stood next to a car. He explained it was his first day of his job working as a translator for the government. On the back of this photograph was his name, phone number & address. The young 20 year old me took the photo of the young 20 year old him and placed it in my travel diary, where it has sat for the last 10 years.

Now 10 years on, as me and Erin embark on our huge life changing trip, we have decided to try and track this man down. We start by dialling the telephone number on the hotel phone only to be met with a gut wrenching long “beeeeeeeeeep” 
We then asked the hotel staff to try the number for us on their phones, they gave us the same answer “this phone is no longer active”. Our next and final option was to order a grab (with the help of our new hotel staff friends) to the address on the photograph. We did not know if he even still lived here but we had to try. 

Nervous energy filled both of our bodies as the grab driver got us closer to our destination. Our next job after arriving into a very local Vietnamese area and leaving the confused looking grab drivers car, was to find his building. 
This was proving much tougher than expected, we started to ask local people for help were either met with “no”, a loose finger pointing direction or equal confusion. 

After 20 minutes of asking we had attracted a lot of attention to ourselves in the streets as residents were watching, this actually ended up playing to our advantage as a lovely woman who spoke great English saw us and gave us the help we needed to guide us to the exact area we needed to be in. 

Another show of the picture I had to a local shopkeeper got us to the finish line as she replied “You want to find Ms.Kim?” Our faces filled with excitement, joy and nerves as she started to ring this person, explaining that two foreigners were looking for her husband. 

In between Ms.Kim arriving, the young lady shopkeeper told me that the man I was looking for had passed away. We were both in a rollercoaster of emotions and this was heartbreaking news. His wife walked around the corner with confusion as she was met with us but I showed her the photo of her husband in his youthful days as a smile burst on her face. 

She sadly told me (in Vietnamese, which was then loosely translated by the shop keeper and then thoroughly translated by Tony a member of staff at the hotel - thank you!!) that he passed away in early 2015, not 6 months after I met him. 

It was truly was a heartwarming and heartbreaking experience but to have met his wife and let her know that her husbands life still exists in other ways was truly beautiful. 

To follow our journey past and future please feel free to like, subscribe and share this story

description:
10 years ago in 2014, I (a 20 year old Jason) was travelling through Vietnam, more specifically to this story Hanoi. 

One night, I was sat on a tiny stool in a street bar next to a busy road filled with only locals. I got chatting to this table of older Vietnamese men, who then invited us (me and my new friends Fraser and Orla) to sit with them. I don’t remember much of what we talked about with those men, but I do remember it being wholesome. 

Before we parted ways one of the men (Tao was his name) gave me an old photograph of his younger self stood next to a car. He explained it was his first day of his job working as a translator for the government. On the back of this photograph was his name, phone number & address. The young 20 year old me took the photo of the young 20 year old him and placed it in my travel diary, where it has sat for the last 10 years.

Now 10 years on, as me and Erin embark on our huge life changing trip, we have decided to try and track this man down. We start by dialling the telephone number on the hotel phone only to be met with a gut wrenching long “beeeeeeeeeep” 
We then asked the hotel staff to try the number for us on their phones, they gave us the same answer “this phone is no longer active”. Our next and final option was to order a grab (with the help of our new hotel staff friends) to the address on the photograph. We did not know if he even still lived here but we had to try. 

Nervous energy filled both of our bodies as the grab driver got us closer to our destination. Our next job after arriving into a very local Vietnamese area and leaving the confused looking grab drivers car, was to find his building. 
This was proving much tougher than expected, we started to ask local people for help were either met with “no”, a loose finger pointing direction or equal confusion. 

After 20 minutes of asking we had attracted a lot of attention to ourselves in the streets as residents were watching, this actually ended up playing to our advantage as a lovely woman who spoke great English saw us and gave us the help we needed to guide us to the exact area we needed to be in. 

Another show of the picture I had to a local shopkeeper got us to the finish line as she replied “You want to find Ms.Kim?” Our faces filled with excitement, joy and nerves as she started to ring this person, explaining that two foreigners were looking for her husband. 

In between Ms.Kim arriving, the young lady shopkeeper told me that the man I was looking for had passed away. We were both in a rollercoaster of emotions and this was heartbreaking news. His wife walked around the corner with confusion as she was met with us but I showed her the photo of her husband in his youthful days as a smile burst on her face. 

She sadly told me (in Vietnamese, which was then loosely translated by the shop keeper and then thoroughly translated by Tony a member of staff at the hotel - thank you!!) that he passed away in early 2015, not 6 months after I met him. 

It was truly was a heartwarming and heartbreaking experience but to have met his wife and let her know that her husbands life still exists in other ways was truly beautiful.

description:
We’re on a mission to find the best Vietnamese football shirts, and that means some serious haggling. 

During our stay in Vietnam we decided to head out to the local shops and markets that Hanoi has to offer. In most parts of the old quarter you cannot walk down the street without seeing football shirts from leagues/countries all over the world… Manchester City, PSG, Inter Miami to teams closer to where we were staying. 
BUT as we were in Vietnam we wanted to show support to the local teams, so we are on the hunt for either the national team or Hanoi FC. 

We walked the streets of the old quarter in the blistering heat trying to find the best football shirt, best quality, best fit and most importantly best PRICE! 

Every time we found the best fitting shirt it was too expensive and they weren’t budging on price and every time we found the best price, it was a bad fit or poor quality. Persistence finally pays off and Jason (after trying on many shirts in the middle of the shop and exposing his chest to the general public) finally finds a cool looking Hanoi FC shirt that fits well and at a fair price.

If you’re still reading this, please like this video and subscribe to our channel for more.

description:
In this video we experience trying the Filipino fast food restaurant “Jollibee” in Vietnam. 
We decided to find the nearest Jollibee to us in Hanoi which is located in the Vincom Shopping centre. After arriving at this very modern shopping centre, we headed up the escalators right to the top, until we saw the famous Jollibee logo! 
We ordered a few things off the menu to compare and also a few things off the menu that we hadn’t seen before to try them out. 
We couldn’t really taste a massive difference in the menu, the chicken seemed to be a lot bigger in Vietnam but the amazing taste of the spaghetti was still present as were all of the flavours that make Jollibee so great in the Philippines!

description:
We really wanted to try Tokyo's Michelin Star ramen at Nakiryu. We knew it was going to be busy but we had no idea you had to get a ticket at 8am for the shop opening at 11am so we got there just after 11am and all the tickets were sold out!! So after this failed attempt, we headed to Ramen Street underneath Tokyo Station to get our ramen fix as we didn't have time to go back (this time!). 

Ramen Street has 8 shops all serving... you guessed it, RAMEN! The idea behind the street is to bring together many different types of ramen and every shop puts their own unique spin on their ramen, from different toppings, noodles or sauce - every ramen is different so you never get bored! 

We chose one at random and chose one that specialises in seafood ramen and kelp soy sauce. We had just enough cash to get us two bowls of their standard ramen. We queued up for about 10 minutes outside and then once we were seated, our ramen came out straight away. It was so delicious but sadly not Michelin rated!

title: Have Tourists RUINED Tsukiji Fish Market? #tokyo #japan #japanesefood #japantravel #foodie #tsukiji
