tags: ancient egypt|valley of the kings|king tuts tomb|tutankhamun|tutankhamun tomb|luxor 2021|travel|vlog|travel vlog|adventure vlog|outdoor adventure|egypt vlog|egyptian vlog|king tut tomb|finding king tuts tomb|egypt exploring|nile river|nile exploring|valley of the kings secret|valley of the kings secret tomb|secret tombs|luxor egypt|egyptian tombs|queen hatshepsut|hatshepsut temple|travelgramers egypt|history documentary|ancient egypt documentary
description:
* How to get to Valley of the Kings from Luxor?
If you are staying in the east bank we recommend that you cross the river by the public ferry that only costs 1EP if you are Egyptian and 5 if you are foreigner and once you are on the west bank you can take a taxi or a tuk-tuk, we went by tuk tuk and he charged us 70EP to go and come back, we agreed a time with him to pick us up. Alternatively you can take a tour which will not only take you to Valley of the Kings but other tourist attractions, the tour can be with the driver only or you can also hire a guide, any hotel can arrange this for you but if you are on a budget like us it won't be cheap.
* How much does it cost to visit Valley of the Kings?
As for now the price is 240EP per person plus 4EP per person for a short train ride from the ticket office to the tombs area (there's no option to walk you have to pay the 4EP lol) this ticket gives you access to 3 tombs of your choice, there are 9 tombs open to tourists out of the 60 + found at the valley, not all the 9 tombs are open at the same time as they close some from time to time to do some restoration and to minimise the deterioration. We recommend that you ask before going what tombs are open to visit as there is a an information board at the entrance of the valley and previous visitors and hotels will be able to give you this info so you can choose the tombs you want to visit and read about them before going.
There's also 3 extra tombs that you have to pay separately if you want to visit Seti I - 1000EP |  Tutankhamun - 300EP | Ramesses V & VI - 100EP
we decided to visit Tutankhamun as his mummy is inside and this was an unique opportunity for us, we have heard that Seti I is an amazing tomb but we didn't have the budget for it plus we were more interested in King's Tut anyway.
* BRIEF HISTORY LESSON 
Egypt was once divided into to kingdoms, the lower Egypt which is north of Egypt and upper Egypt which is the south. 5000 years ago the two kingdoms were united and the pharaohs started ruling it. 
There were 170 pharaohs over 31 dynasties, not all pharaohs were native Egyptian as at some point invaders like the Persians and Greeks would succeed in battles and would take over the thrones. Pharaohs believed they were living gods and that’s why after their death they would build the pyramids and be buried beneath. The pyramids served as a worshipping place so people could still worship their pharaohs after death. This changed around 3500 years ago when the New Kingdom started and Luxor (back then called Thebes) became the capital of ancient Egypt and the pharaohs stopped building pyramids because they wanted a better way to conceal their graves from robbers and also because the funerary practices had changed. As you know pharaohs were mummified and buried with many riches as they believed in the after life and that the body was the home of the soul, if the body was destroyed the soul would be lost that’s why they chose a secret location to hide their tombs - the Valley of the Kings.
The valley of the kings is an elaborate underground complex of tombs were the pharaohs and high elites from the 18th 19th and 20th dynasty would be buried. The valley of the kings it’s still being excavated and studied until today, so far more than 60 tombs have been discovered not all from Pharaohs tho. The pharaohs were buried with everything they possibly needed for the afterlife like gold and miniature boats, furniture, clothes, food, drinks...
Now let's talk about Tutankhamun
Everyone has heard of Tutankhamun is the most famous mummy pharaoh now, not because he was more famous than other pharaohs during his time but because his tomb was one of the most well intact ever found, meaning that people could study it, and uncover more about ancient Egypt more than ever. There is something eerie about Tutankhamun’s tomb tho - an alleged curse, the curse of pharaohs is a curse to be cast upon anyone who disturbs the tomb of a pharaoh, causing bad luck and even death. So allegedly the English man and his team who found the tomb in the succeeding years were “attacked” by this curse and some died on odd circumstances, you can look this up on google for a better coverage.
Tutankhamun’s burial chamber is small and the least decorated it’s believed it's because he died so young at 19 years old and his death wasn't expected so his chamber was a bit rushed nevertheless everything here is very well preserved.

description:
In this video we took a bus from Hurghada to Luxor. Firstly we would like to apologise for the shakiness and quality of the video, we had our bags and we just wanted to document our journey and we didn't focus so much on trying to hold the camera still 😅 Anyways... Like we were saying we took a bus from Hurghada to Luxor, it's about 300km and it takes roughly 5 hours. There are currently no buses leaving in the morning and the earliest one leaves at 3:35pm and arrives at 8:30pm. There are a few companies where you can buy your tickets from but we were recommended by our hotel host GoBus and it costs 145EP per person. After leaving Hurghada until we arrived to Qena (a city before Luxor) we were literally in the middle of the desert and all we could see was sand and rocky mountains or more like hills, one of the best sceneries we've seen in our entire lives plus we got to witness a wicked sunset. After we had dinner was time to go to the West Bank as Luxor is divided into East Bank and West Bank, our accommodation was located in the west bank so we needed to take a ferry, the bridge is quite far from the centre and the preferred method of crossing is by public ferry, we weren't sure where the ferry was departing from since on maps me it was showing one location but it didn't look like there was any ferries from there so we started walking and saw 3 locals guys and asked them where the location was, they walked with us to the public ferry port and even paid for our tickets, 5EP each. Hey hey hey
This video is about our travel day from Istanbul Turkey to Hurghada Egypt.
We were staying in Kadikoy the asian side of Istanbul and our flight was departing from Istanbul airport on the european side, there are buses going to Istanbul airport from the mini bus station next to the ferry port in Kadikoy and it costs 32 lira per person.
After we arrived at the airport we were surprised to see that it was busier than what we expected but clean and hand disinfectant is available literally everywhere.

After we showed our PCR test and completed a health form with our details we were allowed to then go to immigration and everything was very smooth without any problems or questions.
Outside the airport in Hurghada there's no public transport to the city centre so we had to take a taxi, a friendly local helped us calling a UBER, at that time we didn't want to haggle prices with the taxi drivers outside the airport we were too tired for that.

tags: turkey lockdown|corona virus|pcr test|pcr test explained|pcr test for travel|pcr test turkey|pcr test istanbul airport|travel vlog|covid-19 test|covid-19 testing what to expect|covid-19 pcr test|coronavirus test|travel turkey istanbul|travel turkey covid|coronavirus turkey hospital|pcr test how its done|pcr test how to take sample|pcr test how to|travelling to egypt|travelling to egypt during covid
description:
LINKS FOR ALL THE OFFICIAL INFO WE'LL MENTION BELOW WILL BE AT THE END OF THIS PAGE
Travelling abroad nowadays it's kind of different than what it used to be before and because we are still doing it we can give you some insight of what is looks like and what are the procedures and everything you need to know - be aware that things can change pretty quickly without prior notice.
 
There's not many countries open for tourism at the moment and the few that are require a PCR Covid-19 negative test from the tourists and some even require some quarantine time.
So we are going to Egypt and the requirements the Egyptian Gov has in place at the moment are: (this is by no means an exhaustive list)
- having a PCR negative test 72 hours before departure time of country of origin, in english and with a few more specifications (link for that will be below)
-  complete a health declaration form provided by the airline (during the flight)
We needed to get the PCR test, obviously, and we could have got it on arrival in Egypt (some airports offer that possibility but not all, please check the links below for all the official info) or we could have also done it before departing, at the airport in Istanbul, but we decided to do it 48 hours before our flight, why? because we would get the results in 24 hours or less and if we happened to have the virus we could have changed the flights date, since most if not all airlines are having this policy of allowing people to change their flights dates and destinations at least once free of charge, only paying extra if the new flight or dates were more expensive than the original one.
Anyway, there's many clinics and hospitals in Istanbul doing the tests, some charge ridiculous prices and some offer the standard which is 250TL, some even go to your accommodation and most hotels in Istanbul can arrange this but most will require an extra fee. 
We had no idea where to go so our friends Steve and Gokçe from @TravelInteresante came into our rescue (thanks so much guys) and recommended us this clinic Biruni Laboratories (link will be below), they have a few different locations and because we were staying in Kadikoy we went to the one is Uskudar and everyone was friendly and professional, they could speak good English and explained us everything from how long was the test going to take, how long to get the results, how we were going to get the results... 
The results were sent via email in both English and Turkish and we got them in less than 24 hours, don't forget to bring your passport as you will need it to fill in some forms - whatever clinic or hospital you go you'll need your passport. 
And that's pretty much it on this video, after we done the test (which was not a good experience btw lol) we went for a walk and to drink some warm drinks by sea, that same evening Cristiana got her results back and the next morning (early morning) Joao got his and they were both NEGATIVE.

title: The oldest temple in the world - Göbekli Tepe / 12000 year's old

description:
Please find all the information needed below to get to Gobekli Tepe using public transport.

"Gobekli Tepe presents monumental round-oval and rectangular megalithic structures erected by hunter-gatherers in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic age between 9,600 and 8,200 BCE. These monuments were probably used in connection with rituals, most likely of a funerary nature. Distinctive T-shaped pillars are carved with images of wild animals, providing insight into the way of life and beliefs of people living in Upper Mesopotamia about 11,500 years ago."
Gobekli Tepe was erected by hunter-gatherers in the neolithic time, until this monumental structures were found we all believed that hunters were just that and didn't have the time, energy or even the thoughts to put into something like this (basically people thought the neolithic men were "cave-men") but Gobekli Tepe just came to prove this wrong. 
People were much more than hunters and were already performing some kind of rituals or funerals for the deceased much earlier than anticipated, 6 million years earlier to be more precise. 
All of this happened before farming and writing was invented and these guys were already carving rocks and building these huge structures. 
There's not much the archaeologists know about this site and there's a lot of theories around it but one thing is for sure Gobekli Tepe at 12,000 years old predated humanity's oldest known civilisations. 
It's megalithic temples were cut from rock millennia before the 4,500-year-old pyramids in Egypt, 5,000-year-old Stonehenge in England, or 7,000-year-old Nabta Playa, the oldest known astronomical site, Gobekli Tepe came to revolutionise everything we thought we knew.  

https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1572/

https://goo.gl/maps/WJckxU4etCkt7RecA
The bus is bus number zero and there's a couple of bus stops in Urfa where the bus passes and those bus stops will have a poster of Gobekli Tepe (once you see one you will know the bus stops there) and the bus leaves the bus stop in front of urfa museum before passes through the bus station but the easier way is to head to the bus station where you can also get buses to the airport.
If you use maps.me app you can also find all of this there.
At the time of our visit there was only two bus journey a day to go and another two to come back
to go (gobekli Tepe) it was at 10am and 2pm
to come back (urfa) it was at 12pm and 4pm
you can find the time schedule on the bus stops and bus station mentioned above but please check before you go and don't rely on our info since things can change.

The rock formations are the result of a volcanic eruption that took place 2 million years ago (even tho we found articles stating 60 million years we are more inclined to believe the 2 million), the rocks have this weird shape because of the wind and rain, the erosion process created this magnificent shapes and the people that were settled here discovered that the rocks could be "easily" carved and started carving the rocks and building homes, castles, places of worship and so on.

title: The Lost City of Ephesus - All you need to know
tags: temple of artemis|ephesus turkey|ancient city|ephesus during covid|travelling turkey during covid|ephesus|ephesus the 7 churches of revelation|all you need to know ephesus|grand theater ephesus|ephesus travel guide|ephesus (city/town/village)|library of celsus turkey|ephesus vlog|roman ruins|turkey 2020|what to see turkey|travelgramers turkey|ephesus video|turkey (country)|ephesus ancient city|ephesus turkey documentary|ephesus turkey ancient city
description:
Hello peeps in this video we visited Ephesus, one of the most visited places in Turkey, now during low winter season and with covid19 around there was absolutely no tourists and we had the place just to ourselves so we had the time to appreciate and understand this magnificent ancient city, but what is Ephesus?
We will explain it very briefly as the history is long and complex:
Ephesus was a city port founded by the greeks, (the whole coast of todays Turkey was in fact part of ancient Greece during the Classical Greek Era), in the 10th century BCE. 
In 129 BCE the Roman Empire took over the city and because of this most of what we see in Ephesus today is from the Roman era. 
The city of Ephesus was once considered the most important Greek city, the most important trading center in the Mediterranean region and one of the richest cities, Ephesus made all its money from trade and with advanced building knowledge they built one of the greatest cities in the world that still "stands" today (some of it anyway). 
Around the 15th century AD Ephesus was abandoned and the main reason for this was silt build up in the harbour, which eventually reached the point where no ship could reach the city, the city was also destroyed before this and since then was never the same and started to decline but even after nearly 3 millennia Ephesus left it's legacy to archaeologists, historians and the thousands of visitors to come to the region each year to see the ancient ruins.
Excavations started around the 18 hundreds and ONLY 15% of it has been excavated, meaning that the remain 85% is still underground, if with 15% revealed we were left speechless we can only imagine how magnificent Ephesus was once before if we had the chance to see it all.
Hope you enjoy the video and that it brings you some knowledge about Ephesus.

description:
Hello peeps in this video we show you the Basilica of St John, the ayasuluk castle, the aqueduct and the temple of Artemis, all of this located in Selcuk. 
We speak about the history of the sites and we bring you along with us to a different time and era. 
"Ayasuluk Hill is an ancient mount in İzmir Province in Turkey. It forms part of the Ephesus UNESCO World Heritage Site, and is home to a Byzantine fortress and the ruins of the Basilica of St John. It was reputedly the tomb of John the Evangelist, an early disciple of Jesus who is thought to have written the Gospel of John on the site. It became the main settlement of Ephesus after the ancient town declined after the 7th century, following the onset of the Arab–Byzantine wars.
The earliest archaeological remains at the site date to the Hittite era of the 2nd millennium BC, when the site was known as Apasa. There is also evidence of some Mycenaean presence before the start of the Helladic period around 1050 BC. The hill is known to be the original location of Ephesus, before it moved to a new location a few kilometers away."
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayasuluk_Hill

"The aqueducts were built in the Byzantine Era to carry the spring water near the east of Selçuk to St John Basilica and the settlements around it which are 50 meters up from the sea level. Marble blocks from Ephesus and Artemision were brought here to be reused. The abutments are 15 meters high."
https://visitephesus.org/en/where-to-visit/byzantine-aqueduct/

"One of the Seven Wonders of the World in ancient times, the Temple of Artemis (Artemision) at Ephesus was a famous place of pilgrimage for centuries and it was built dedicated to Artemis. Anatolia has always had a fertility goddess: Mita to the Phrygians, Cybele (or Kybele) to many other Anatolian peoples, Artemis to the Greeks and Diana to the Romans.Unfortunately little remains of the vast, rich marble temple: only a few bits of marble column favored by the storks who arrive in the nearby town of Selçuk each spring. There’s not a lot to see, but it’s worth dropping in at the Artemision ruins on the 3-km (2-mile, 30-minute) walk from Selçuk to the Ephesus archeological site along shady Dr Sabri Yayla Boulevard."

description:
Hello everyone, in this video we travelled from Istanbul otogar (main bus station) to Selçuk in Izmir province.
Currently there's a lockdown on weekends for the locals and residents but this doesn't apply to tourists so since we were done with Istanbul we decided it was time to move to our next destination, it happened to be on a weekend and we thought this journey was going to be easy and smooth but it wasn't really easy.
We had to check out from our hotel in Istanbul at 12pm so we grabbed something to eat before leaving the hotel and headed to the otogar main bus station which is 10km away from sultanahmet area, we took public transportation and when we arrived to the bus station we went through our 1st police check point, they asked us to see our passports and where we were going, after we answered they let us go wishing us a safe trip.
We manage to buy a bus ticket not to selcuk but to Izmir 70km away so we thought once in Izmir we would be able to find buses going to selcuk right? - Wrong. 
Our bus from istanbul to Izmir was saturday night 11pm, we spent the whole afternoon waiting for our bus on the bus station, many places to grab some food were open. As we were sitting on the waiting room we went through our 2nd police check, this time 4 police officers came to us and asked the same things - passport and where we were going, after checking we were tourists they wished us a safe trip and carried out with their work.
We arrived in Izmir at around 8am sunday, upon arrival we realised everything on the bus station was closed literally everything, we walked around and there was nobody to ask questions, and this is when a police officer spotted us and came to talk to us. We explained where we wanted to go and with his poor english we said there was no buses on the weekends so our best option was to go by train but to get to the train station we needed to use either a taxi (which is usually very expensive) or we could take a city bus but for that we needed to buy a card, all of this was sounding very confusing to us specially after 8 or 9 hours on an overnight bus but we were whiling to try but the police officer probably realised we were not going to make it on our own we sent another police officer to help us out to buy the pass for the city bus and to show us where the bus stop was. This was the best that could ever have happened and we can't thank these police officers enough.
After being on the city bus we needed to figure out where we needed to get out, we tried asking the bus driver but the poor man couldn't understand what we were saying and again another kind soul stepped up and told us to follow him as he was going to the train station and he would show us where to go.
We are 100% sure if it wasn't for the kind souls we encounter we wouldn't have make it to Selcuk and we would be so frustrated.
We have leant our lesson and next time we are going from A to B we will go on a weekday to avoid these struggles, in a way we are glad we did this because we got to see how kind and helpful Turkish people are.

Turkey has implemented a weekend lockdown from 4th of December for Turkish citizens and residents. The lockdown on weekends starts from 9pm on fridays and ends at 5am on mondays and people are only allowed out to buy essentials, there's also a nightly curfew on weekdays from 9pm to 5am but the restrictions above don't apply to tourists, meaning we can go out anytime. - Public transportation is operating as usual (so it seemed)
- Very few places who serve food are open (but you can always find something so don't worry you won't starve)
- Locals and residents are complying to the restrictions, everyone we saw out today were all tourists and the occasional guy walking his dog, feeding the stray cats, going to/from work or grabbing some essentials from the corner shop (fines apply for those who don't and police is always on the look-out, again tourists are exempt from this rule)

description:
In this video we visited the most well known tourist attractions of Istanbul and we were not disappointed by what Istanbul has to offer.
The history of Istanbul dates back to 3 thousand years ago so to deeply understand it we will need to read A LOT, from the times where Istanbul was known as Lygos to the byzantine empire and then the Ottoman empire, there’s a lot to cover but we like history. 
For the ones interested in reading we will leave a link here in regards to the history of Istanbul, again it’s long.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Istanbul
Today we will keep it simple and one can not come to Istanbul and not visit the most well known tourist attractions so today we will start with that.
We’re going to do a walking tour by ourselves and we’re going to cover Hagia Sofia, Grand Baazar, Blue Mosque, Spice Baazar and Galata Bridge so let’s go it’s going to be a busy day.

First stop is the Blue Mosque, the original name is Sultan Ahmet Mosque so why do we and everyone else calls it Blue Mosque?
The answer is inside, the tiles are blue and the Mosque was starting to be built in 1609, this mosque is also a classical style of Ottoman architecture with Byzantine influence. 

Next stop is Hagia Sofia (AYA SOPHIA) a Unesco World Heritage Site, Hagia Sofia was built in 537 so is more than one thousand years old and it was the was back then then the largest Christian church of the the Byzantine Empire.
Without the modern tools and technology we have nowadays this was an amazing construction done more than 1 thousand years ago.
Originally was built as a church but it has changed throughout the centuries
In the 14hundreds was converted into a mosque during the Ottoman empire and in the 1930s was converted into a museum until this year 2020 when was then converted back into a functioning mosque. 
If you visit Aya Sofya expect to see and admire both Christian and Islamic elements inside.
We were astonished by how beautiful the architecture is, the large interior, the high ceilings, the splendid chandeliers and columns, it’s hard to find the right words to describe it and it’s easily one of the most beautiful buildings we’ve had the pleasure of visiting. 

Next stop is the Grand Bazaar, is one of the largest and oldest covered markets in the world with more than 5 thousand shops and employing around 26,000 people.
This market was an important trading centre in the 15th century, so in other words the first shopping mall of Istanbul and probably the world.

After the Grans Bazaar we went to the Spice bazaar it is the most famous covered shopping complex after the Grand Bazaar.

Next and last stop is Galata bridge, the reason this is a tourist attraction is because of the views that it offers over the city on both sides of the strait, this strait is called Bosphorus or Bosporus strait.

title: What's like to fly during a Pandemic
tags: turkish airlines|flying to turkey|flying to turkey during covid|flying to turkey vlog|flying to turkey covid 19|turkey is open to tourists|flying during covid 19|flying during pandemic|malaysia|leaving malaysia during mco|travelgramers malaysia|flying during coronavirus|travel vlog|is safe to travel right now|is it safe to travel to turkey 2020|is it safe to travel to turkey|how to travel|how to travel cheap
description:
In this video we show you what it's like to fly during this pandemic.
We took a flight from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia where we've been for the past 10 months to Istanbul, Turkey.
Turkey is the few countries that has opened up for tourism and after so long we Malaysia we started to have itchy feet and decided to book a flight to Turkey, we were afraid that our flight would get cancelled or that we would have issues entering Turkey or leaving Malaysia after so long staying under a tourist visa but despite our nervousness and anxiety everything went very smooth. 

CHECK IN PROCESS
To check in to our flight the usual procedures were applied nothing new or different here (some countries like UK requires people to fill in a health form online 48 hours prior to arrival so people going to destinations requiring this would have to present this to the check in counter staff, in our case this was not applied since Turkey doesn't require any health forms to be filled in before arrival).

IMMIGRATION - STAMP OUT
At the immigration counter in Malaysia they asked us why we have overstayed for so long, the reason was lockdown and since the government in Malaysia gave permission to all foreigners staying under tourist visa to stay until the end of the MCO - Movement Control Order (lockdown in other words)(end of MCO is now 31/12/20) we decided to stay for as long as we could and wanted. They filled in a form for us to sign stating the reason for overstaying and stamped us out, we were not black listed or anything so we can always go back after this pandemic is over and Malaysia opens up for tourism.
After this was time for the metal detector which was completely empty, there was no queues and after the metal detector the corridors of the airport were empty, all shops were closed and it was very strange to be there and seeing an airport like that. 
We had to go through another metal detector to enter our gate, again very easy and only the people going in the same flight as us were there.
Before entering the plane we were given a hygiene pack with hand sanitiser, antiseptic wipes and face masks, we found our seats and took off.

DURING THE FLIGHT 
It's mandatory to use face masks at all times during the flight a part from when we are eating, we were not given any face shields or anything. The flight was not full there was plenty of empty seats and rows, our row was full so we asked if we could chose another seat were we could have a row for ourselves but this wasn't allowed due to covid19 measures we were told the a member of the cabin crew, we didn't understand why but it made sense later on when they gave us a health form to complete and give to the immigration officers in Istanbul where one of the questions were our seat number, I guess this is in case someone falls ill they would know how was seated near that person.
I guess this flight was not as strict as other flights from other parts of the world since Malaysia has been dealing with the virus pretty good so face shields and cabin crew members dressed in white suits were not required.
The food on out flight was a bit disappointing since we didn't have a hot meal and the sandwiches were not the best quality ones (this was a Turkish airlines flight so we had our expectations high).
A lot of people during the flight were taking their face masks off and the cabin crew was often asking people to put them back on, that was annoying because I would be sleeping and it would be a complete silent airplane when I would wake up to a member of the cabin crew talking to a person in the same area of where we were seated asking them to put the mask back on, they made several announcements during the flight but some people didn't care.
The toilets were cleaned very often like every 30 minutes or 1 hour depending on how busy the toilets were, they would also clean the doors and handles of the toilets almost every time after someone used it.

IMMIGRATION - ON ARRIVAL TO A NEW COUNTRY
Ok, this is the final step, arriving in cold Istanbul and going through immigration there, super easy and stress free - we gave them the health form filled in (flight number, seat number, if we were in contact with someone with covid19 recently, these type of questions), and they stamped us in. The whole process was super easy and nothing seemed to have changed that much.
Hope this is helpful to anyone who wants or is thinking of travelling to a country that is open for tourism right now.

title: Artisans of Malaysia the art of hand made goods
tags: keris|kris|keris making|malaysia|terengganu|songket weaving malaysia|songket malaysia|keris making process|traditional keris making|songket weaving terengganu|wau making|kite making|flying wau|malaysia 2020|artisans of malaysia|artisans of terengganu|dying arts and crafts|traditional|malay culture|travelgramers|malaysia 2020 tourism
description:
Terengganu is full of surprises and artisans, people here kept their traditions very much alive and it's what we're going to see today.
Our first stop of the day was to see how keris is made. 
"Keris for the ones who don't know is an "asymmetrical dagger with distinctive blade-patterning achieved through alternating laminations of iron and nickel iron. The kris is famous for it's distinctive wavy blade, although many have straight blades as well. Keris is also a symbol of power and of ethnic pride. Kris is also one of the weapons commonly used in Pencak Silat martial art, which is also native to the region. Keris or Kris is also part of the men wedding attire. Keris making is considered as a dying art in Malaysia, however visit to the keris making centre in Kampung Pasir Panjang and Kampung Ladang Titian in Kuala Terengganu is still worth. Here you can see how a piece of raw iron is to turn into this significance and meaning rich weapon. You can also purchase you own piece of keris collection with relatively cheap price."

Our second stop was to see songket weaving, songket is a cloth that the men traditionally use around their waist. "It is hand-woven in silk or cotton, and intricately patterned with gold or silver threads. The metallic threads stand out against the background cloth to create a shimmering effect.
Songket is a brocade, where gold and silver threads are woven on a cotton or silk base where the motifs “float” to form beautiful pieces. Considered a luxury textile, its place in Malay culture is regarded as a must-wear for ceremonial dresses and costumes, worn by both men and women. The production of a songket piece can take weeks or months depending on its length and the intricate patterns that are employed.
Songket is traditionally considered an exquisite, luxurious and prestigious traditional fabric.
Songket is one of Terengganu’s top products whose weavers are considered to be the best in the country.
Depending on the grade of the songket, which is determined by the intricate weft and patterns, pieces can fetch a very high price, some as high as RM80,000 or more. However, most pieces are priced between RM500 to RM8000. It is often handed down to family members as heirlooms."

Our third and final stop was to see a wau or kite maker.
"Wau  (pronounce as ‘wow’) can appear in all shapes and size but the most popular and famous kite is the moon kite (wau bulan) and cat kite (wau kucing) in the east coast. Kite making requires patience and tremendous skill. Bamboo will be cut and make into the frame or skeleton of the kite. The best time to cut the bamboo is in November or December and this will be kept for 10 months before it is split and soaked in water followed by heated to straighten and toughen. On the other hand, designs are traced on a tinted and shiny glazed paper and then carefully cut out and pasted on paper which is glued to the bamboo skeleton. The designs are normally flowers with vines which signifies women (flower) and man (vine), eg. if the flowers are in bud form, it symbolises a young woman etc. In some older designs, flowers were drawn from the side and back to represent the shy and reserved personality of female in those days whereas for the vines, the more meandering the vines, the more twists and turns in a man’s life. There are also waus that are made using the batik technique or painted by batik artists and the designs are always more creative and less formalised by tradition.It is never an easy job to fly a Wau kite into the sky. A traditional Wau can be as big as 3.5m in height and 2.5 m wing span and usually needs the help of a group of person to bring it to the sky. In a windy day, a Wau can fly up to 450m into the sky. To choose a good kite, you should look at the harmonious colours matched and the flowers as well as the vines drawn which represent the inner state of the kite maker."

description:
Hello everyone in this video we visited Kampung Budaya Terengganu - Terengganu Cultural Village located at the Terengganu Museum where the 8 districts (Besut, Setiu, Hulu Terengganu, Kuala Nerus, Kuala Terengganu, Marang, Dungun and Kemaman) are represented since the concept of the Cultural Village is a living museum and highlights all the traditional arts, culture and heritage found in eight districts in the state. 
We think it's a great place for people to visit and learn more about Terengganu in just one place. 
We visited some boats that were used back in the days by sailors and traders, the boats were restored and are now part of the Cultural Village, we tried keropok fried in hot sand (delicious by the way) as back in the days people sometimes didn't have oil so they used hot sand instead, got to know the history behind the name of the famous market in Terengganu - Pasar Payang, did you know that the market got it's name because the fishermen used to park their boats by the market area and the boats were called payang and that area gained it's name Pasar (market) Payang (the name of the boats), more interesting things were visiting old traditional malay houses that were also restored, we also saw how they harvest and get the rice grains out of the rice grass, played traditional games, we even had the opportunity to dress up in traditional Malay and Terengganu wedding attire, the last activity was to play gamelan (a multi-timbre ensemble consisting of metallophones, xylophones, flutes, gongs, voices, as well as bowed and plucked strings) we were not very good at it but still have loads of fun.
We leant a lot about Malay culture so we highly recommend visiting.

description:
Hello everyone in this video we witnessed something pretty cool.
Gasing Terbang or flying tops, have you heard of it? Probably yes if you are from Malaysia, if you are not, allow us to quickly explain:
Gasing Terbang is a game where one person throws the spinning top that weights 4kg onto a platform, that spinning top then flies off of that platform that is normally elevated from the ground and then a second person tries to catch the top/disk whilst it's up in the air, the reason the spinning top flies off of the platform is because the man who throws it uses such a amazing technique, first he throws the spinning top and as the top is nearly touching the platform he pulls the rope and then magic happens.
These tops/disks then spin for approximately 2 hours and the team that gets the top/disk to spin the longest time wins. 
All of this sounds easy right? Wrong! There's a lot of technique, strength and preparation involved, these gentlemen use a rope that is stretched and covered with a sticky substance and the most incredible thing about this sport is that the top is caught up in the air.
This is one of the things that are best explained and understood when you actually see it and that's why you shouldn't be reading this but watching the video 😜
Anyway after watching the gentleman performing or showing us the game we had a go at battling tops where a young kid put us all to shame, great fun and games but it didn't end there. Do you remember the potatoes that we bought on our previous video? We finally had them in all sort of shapes and forms, in all the possibly aways known to humans. Delicious or should we say Sedap!

description:
Hello everyone and welcome to another vlog in Terengganu, Malaysia.
This time we went to Besut district, we ended up meeting more interesting people and having them sharing their talents and skills with us.
- 00.00.53 Gentlemen weaving and playing Serunao
First we went to Kampung Benting Lintang where we met this gentleman that weaves mats and baskets out of some type of river grass, Alex (one of our guides and the most knowledgeable person on Malaysian history we've ever met) explained us the process and the friendly gentleman even took us to the place where we normally harvests the grass. After a while we discovered that we also plays an instrument called Serunai, similar to a flute but much more interesting, unfortunately the instrument was out of tune and was hard to get it back to tune again so the gentleman only played a little bit for us and we still found it to have a beautiful tune. Surprise, surprise and despite his old age, he also had a mini charcoal factory at the back of his house where we has making some and selling it to the local shops to make a bit more income.
- 00.04.48 Buying potatoes
Second stop of the day was a road side stall selling many different types of potatoes and tubers. We also saw how cassava or tapioca is harvested. We discovered that during rainy season (November to February on the East Coast of Malaysia) people's diet is quite different from when it's dry season, being potatoes and tubers like cassava/tapioca very popular, dry fish also comes to the scene more than ever as fishermen won't be able to go fishing as often due to weather conditions, so with all of that said we had to buy some of the different types of potatoes but unfortunately by the time we got back to the our hotel (Terrapuri Heritage Village) dinner was ready so the potatoes were left to be cooked the next day which will be featured on our next video.
- 00.06.50 Desa Ukiran Kayu 
Next stop was to Desa Ukiran Kayu or Wood Carving Village where there's a gallery with the best work of some of the best wood carver, a Workshop where apprentices can learn how to carve or to improve their skills and a shop where some of the work done is available to buy. It was quite an interesting place as we got to learn the 3 different techniques, Kerawang (pencil carving), Tebuk timbul (kind of 3D carving) and tebuk tembus (open carving, normally used for windows). 
- 00.08.36 Visiting Masjid Russia
Next stop was to visit a mosque that is quite different from the usual mosques, this one looks like the St. Basil's Cathedral in Russia, it was beautiful and worth a visit - kampung Lapan Kotak.
- 00.09.24 Visiting Masjid Kayu
Another quick stop at Masjid Ulul Albab or Masjid kayu (wooden Mosque)
- 00.09.31 gentleman playing a Rebab
This gentleman that we visited was another great surprise for us, it's said that we has healing powers through his music and instrument called Rebab, it was the first time we saw that instrument that looks like a small guitar but it's played like a violin but instead of placing it on the shoulder it just rests on the floor. Another interesting artist that made his own Rebab and played a beautiful song for us.

description:
Pulau Duyong is an island in Kuala Terengganu that hosts a very traditional fishing village where we can still see boats being built or repaired by the skilful locals using an ancient technique.
Miniature versions of the boats are also a famous local business attraction.
Wooden houses and fishes being dried under the sun on the streets are not a rare sight in Pulau Duyong and there’s quite a lot to cover in such a small island. 
From watching the locals getting on with their daily lives to visiting small local businesses and places of undoubtedly beautiful architecture, Pulau Duyong it’s surely a must if your ever in Terengganu. 
During our visit here we had the opportunity to visit Kota Lama, this was once a house turned into a museum, it’s beautiful architecture from different influences including Islamic, Chinese and Western are remarkable. 
Other places worth visiting are a public library, the only one of it’s kind on the Island, this place can serve as a study room for local kids as well as a place of inspiration for adults.

After the busy day unraveling the authenticity of Pulau Duyong we came to stay in Duyong Marina Resort.
Duyong Marina Resort is located in Pulau Duyong Kecil in Kuala Terengganu, it’s a 5 star boutique hotel with 97 chalets and it offers amazing views overlooking Kuala Terengganu. 
This resort is so big that they provide a golfcart shuttle service to and from the restaurant area. 
The resort is located just across from Marina Restaurant/Cafe called Bytes Cafe where we had a Steam Boat for Dinner overlooking the city and it’s worth mentioning that the Restaurant/ Cafe welcomes the general public and not just the guests of the resort. 
Breakfast is also provided so you can start you day the right way, they are proud to serve their local signature dishes but if you are fancying something different there’s plenty of other choices to choose from, for example a light western breakfast. 
The relaxed atmosphere, comfy beds and spectacular views makes it perfect for a great getaway.

description:
Disclaimer - This video was filmed before the new CMCO was implemented.
Since we arrived in Malaysia this time we really explored the Malay culture but we barely scratch the surface of other cultures so today is the day we explored the Chinese culture in Malaysia.
In Malaysia Peranakan means mixed. 
So we can have Peranakans with Chinese ancestery, Peranakans with Indian ancestry, Peranakans with Eurasian ancestry, (in Malacca for example they are called Kristang), Peranakan Indian Muslims, Malay and Arab ancestry.

So now that we got that part explained let's talk about what we did and visited on that day, we started off the day with a nice boat ride along the Terengganu river doing the same route Cheng Ho did when he arrived to Terengganu. Cheng Ho was a muslim admiral, sailor and trader and when he arrived to Terengganu he went up the river to collect some fresh water and the legend says there is a footprint at the bottom of the river so around that location the locals built a temple to pay tribute to him and his arrival, the temple is taoist but because Cheng Ho was muslim at the entrance of the temple there is Jawi script as well as Chinese characters and Malay with the name of the temple. So we got to learn a little bit of the history if Cheng Ho before we headed to another kampung (village) to visit a Peranakan Chinese family and their house and they also cooked us lunch. 
We learnt so much about Peranakan Chinese and they way they live.
After this very insightful day we went to Terrapuri Herritage Village to spend the night.

description:
This is probably a very strange video as we don't normally shoot videos like this so bear with us ;) 

Hello everyone in this video we want to tell you about our decision of leaving Malaysia.

This might sound as sad news but it's something that we have been thinking about for quite some time now and as we've travelling for 3 years this was the longest travel break we've ever had. We were still able to travel around Malaysia but after 10 months here this feels more and more like home.

We were waiting for the lockdown in Kuala Lumpur that took place a couple of weeks ago to be lifted so we could go there and make a final decision of whereas we wanted to stay a bit longer or leave. 
Since KL is not opening anytime soon, in fact another national lockdown is taken place instead, we decided that now it's the right time to start planning our next destination, since we have a lot of time in our hands. 

Many counties have been opening for tourism and that give us some hope that travelling abroad is possible once again and we can find a new country to discover. 
So far we have Turkey and Egypt as our main focus but things can change and we will update you all (with another life update video) once we have made a decision and planned/ prepared everything for our departure.

We are forever grateful to Malaysia and all Malaysians for everything we lived and experienced here and for letting us stay here safe and sound and for such generosity that we encounter every single day, this is not a goodbye as we plan to return to Malaysia again and again, plus we have a couple of more video to release that we were shooting last week with Tourism Terengganu.

description:
In this video we went to Tasik (lake) Kenyir and explored the surroundings there, went for a snack in Kuala Berang to try this famous gigantic roti keramat and visited the place where Inscription Stone was found. 
So now let's break this into places:
Before we even got to Lake Kenyir we stopped on the way to see if we could spot some wildlife, we had Mr. Anuar Mcafee and his family with us showing us the best places to see some incredible animals, we saw this little squirrel,
majestic crested serpent eagle, a dusky leaf monkey, an endangered animal that is Native to Malaysia, Thailand and Myanmar, their newborns are yellow or orange in colour but we didn’t get to spot one this time. 
And now let’s get to the prints, we saw one from a sunbear and one from a Tapir.
"(Tapirs look something like pigs with trunks, but they are actually related to horses and rhinoceroses. This eclectic lineage is an ancient one—and so is the tapir itself. Scientists believe that these animals have changed little over tens of millions of years)" - National Geographic

We didn’t get to see a Rafflesia flower but we went to a spot where there will be one next year around March and we saw the bud where the flower will come out. 

After this wonderful start we then arrived to Lake Kenyir (the biggest artificial lake in southeast asia with 260,000 hectares, created in 1985 by the damming of the Kenyir River. The lake provides water to the Sultan Mahmud Power Station) and went straight (by boat) to one of it's 340 small islands to see the lasir waterfall, then we headed to taman herba (hebal garden), another island where the concept of this place is to preserve and teach the younger generations about medicinal herbs, there are estimate 200 types of traditional herbal species planted there.

Next spot was for a snack in kampung buluh in Kuala Berang, we tried the famous giant roti keramat (Roti Binjai Legend (Kayu Keramat Gergasi)), after our bellies were full we visited the place where The Inscription Stone was found, The Inscription Stone (Batu Bersurat Terengganu) is "is a granite stele carrying Classical Malay inscription in Jawi script that was found in Terengganu, Malaysia. The inscription, dated possibly to 702 AH (corresponds to 1303 CE), constituted the earliest evidence of Jawi writing in the Malay world of Southeast Asia, and was one of the oldest testimony to the advent of Islam as a state religion in the region." - Wikipedia.

With all of this is say goodbye in this video and don't forget to check out Ping Anchorage Travel & Tours social media and website if you want to tour around Malaysia with them.

description:
In this video we explored the Terengganu that people don't usually get to see, but first we started the day in Kuala Terengganu having breakfast at Terradala (http://www.terradala.com/) museum cafe. 
- Our first stop of the day was Jambu Bongkok fishing village (near Marang), a place that is commonly used for movies and dramas sets for it's scenic surroundings. 
- After that we went to melaleuca forest, people here in Malaysia use the wood from the trees to build fences or small pieces of indoor furniture and it's bark is used to seal the gaps between the wood planks on the traditional boats (see this video - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZX9FXXjXxPk Learning Ancient Boat Building Technique).
- The next spot was Kuala Abang beach, a very popular spot amongst the locals in the evenings.
- Turtle stone was also part of our tour, Batu Penyu (Turtle Stone) is located in Bukit Che Hawa, Rantau Abang and the legend says that one day a playful turtle went up the hill but lost it's way and was unable to return and turned into stone, people believe that if the stone is destroyed or disturbed leatherback turtles won't return to the beach located just down the hill to lay eggs, the stone was been in fact disturbed over the years and leatherback turtles are now a extremely rare sight.
- Last but not least spot of the day was to Kampung Batu Puteh to visit a coconut farm and learn how gula melaka is made, gula melaka is a type of sugar made from the flower bud of a coconut palm tree, they cut the flower and collect the liquid that comes out from it, this liquid is then cooked for a few hours until it becomes darker and have a gooey consistency.

Setiu Wetlands
"Nine Ecosystems in One Destination
The Setiu Wetlands consists of three river basins converged to form a continuous lagoon 14 km long. It has nine interconnected ecosystems that read like a biodiversity textbook. It is a mixture of sand islands, mudflats, mangroves, peat swamp, riparian forest, seagrass beds and sand beaches, and a lagoon filled with both sea and fresh water. And its diversity extends to it being a breeding ground for scores of mammals, reptiles and marine life. One can also visit a seafood aquaculture centre in the middle of the lagoon. Not many know that this centre also breeds oysters. Combined with beautiful scenery, Setiu Wetlands is heaven for the eco-tourist – an interesting destination for those who love the outdoors and nature."
https://www.beautifulterengganu.com/where-to-go/setiu-wetlands/setiu-wetlands/

Boat Builders of Terengganu
"Terengganu is well known for its artisanal skills in boat making for centuries. Using no blue prints and no nails, the boat makers are world famous for hand-crafting boats. And we are not just talking about fishing vessels used by our fishermen; bespoke ocean faring wooden boats have been built here. Private individuals from four corners of the world have known to have purchased their boats from our boat makers. Indeed, the skills and craftsmanship of Terengganu boat builders have attracted the attention of many yacht and boat enthusiasts from all over the world.
The skills of these boat builders are highly prized due to their meticulous attention to detail where their crafting is only guided by pure memory and past experience. As mentioned, the original boat builders of the past do not rely on blue prints but their numbers are unfortunately dwindling."

description:
We spent a week in Seremban and visited some of the highlights of this multicultural city.
Seremban is the capital city of the Negeri Sembilan State (not to far from Kuala Lumpur), we found out that Seremban only officially gained it's city status in January 2020 (so quite recently), another curiosity we found out about Seremban is that in the 1500's the Mingankabau people (originally from West Sumatra, Indonesia), settled here and influenced the culture, for example there are some buildings here with a strange and different roof architecture that resembles buffalo horns, this is because Minangkabau comes from a malay expression menang kerbau = winning buffalo.
 Seremban is very multicultural, since we arrived we've seen a big Indian and Chinese community here along with Malay (from mingankabau descendant).

description:
This video is the beginning of a Jungle adventure this time by train, this route is known as the Jungle Train or the The East Coast Line.
We started in Kuala Lipis a town 160km north east of Kuala Lumpur.
Kuala Lipis was a gold-mining centre before the British arrived in 1887.
In 1898, it became the capital of Pahang until 1953. During this time, grand colonial buildings, such as the imposing District Offices and the Clifford School, and the Pahang Club were built. The hilltop house of the British Resident is now a hotel and museum.
The town grew and prospered with the coming of the railway in 1924. However, in August 1955, the state capital was shifted to Kuantan, and Kuala Lipis fell into a decline.
We highly recommend spending at least a day there to visit the old town.

Now onto the train journey...
Part II coming soon...
It runs from Tumpat just north of Kota Bharu in Kelantan down to Gemas in Negeri Sembilan where it joins with the west coast line which runs all the way from Singapore to Bangkok via Johor Bahru, Kuala Lumpur and Penang.
 The name 'East Coast Line' is rather misleading - once the train leaves Tumpat it goes nowhere near the sea. Perhaps it is so-called because it links the east coast state of Kelantan to the rest of Malaysia's rail network. Jungle Railway is a more accurate description because it passes through the sparsely populated and heavily forested interior of Peninsula Malaysia and skirts the Taman Negara and Kenong Rimba national parks.

description:
Looking for a different island vibes in Malaysia? We have the answer - Pulau Tuba.
Pulau means Island in Malay and Tuba is located 5km from Kuah jetty, Langkawi, only a 20min boat journey. It is a beautiful, remote island and the only inhabited islet in the area apart from Langkawi. Here you can experience a genuine local village live, the locals live mainly from fishing and farming and there only a few homestays on the island if you would like to stay the night.
The highlights of Pulau Tuba are cave-exploring and jungle-trekking. You can also spot a variety of wildlife, especially hornbills. We took a few pictures but couldn't get much on video.
If you are not into caves nor jungle trekking Tuba also offers more relaxed options like exploring the island and it's villages and a swim in the beautiful crystal clear waters, we unfortunately chose a wrong day to go there as the weather wasn't the best but still had an amazing day exploring.

Ferry location: 127, Jalan Dato Syed Omar, Kuah, 07000 Langkawi, Kedah

description:
One of the unique things that Brunei has during Hari Raya Aidilfitri — the Muslim festival celebrated to mark the end of Ramadhan — is the ‘open house’ at the Sultan’s palace, Istana Nurul Iman.
Every year, His Majesty and members of the Royal family hold a meet-and-greet (known as ‘junjung ziarah’ in Malay) with the people, opening the palace to the public for three days. The annual event begins on the second day of Eid, and is open not only to Bruneians but to foreigners and tourists who want to experience Hari Raya in Brunei.

tags: 2go ferry|2go travel|Manila to Tablas|manila to cebu|manila to romblon|tablas philippines|tablas island romblon|tablas island|tablas romblon tourist spots|tablas romblon|romblon island|travelgramers philippines|how to travel manila|ferry philippines|ferry manila to bataan|philippines travel vlog|travel philippines 2019|travel philippines|manila philippines|it's more fun in the philippines|ferry manila|romblon
description:
We were staying near the airport so we hoped on a grab and went to Buendia Bus Terminal, there we got a bus to Batangas ferry port (2 hours south of Manila). We didn't book any ferry ticket because we thought we could get a cheaper rate if we booked directly there but it turned out we saved only a couple of dollars and we nearly missed the change to get a space on the ferry, luckily we were able to get tickets for the next morning which meant spending the night in Batangas. 
The ferry port is about 2 or 3 km from the nearest village, we walked there and started to ask the rates of hotels we saw, the cheapest we found was 775 pesos.

Tablas doesn't get many tourists and that's why we decided to start from there, it's not easy to travel in Tablas as the island is not prepared for tourists but the locals are very helpful, many hotels are not online and when we arrived in Odiongan we didn't have anything booked so again we walked around to find accommodation for that night, the city wasn't what we were looking for so the next day we got on a jeepney up north to check an accommodation by the beach called footprints resort, there we could rent a moped and explore the island even tho the people and places surrounding the resort were the best we found in Tablas.

Please note that all ferry ports have a ferry terminal fee that is NOT included in your ticket and has to be paid at the port before embarking. 

We suggest that you get a SIM card for the islands as wifi is non existent, we had a friend that gave us a SMART SIM card and on smart website we found all the packages available, we choose GIGA399 and all we had to do was get to a smart shop and top up the sim card with 400pesos and then the lady help us to set up the package, you can do it in the airport when you arrive, our package works for 30 days and we have unlimited texts, 6 gigs of data and 1gig of youtube everyday.

Hope this video and info is helpful for you and your travels.
Have fun.

title: Malaysia's Little Secret - Labuan Island
tags: labuan island|duty free|labuan malaysia|malaysia island|malaysia duty free|palm beach labuan|labuan beach|maldives of malaysia|brunei to labuan|brunei to labuan ferry|brunei to labuan island|chimney labuan|labuan chimney walking trail|kota kinabalu|travelgramers|labuan marine museum|secret island|labuan island sabah|labuan island nightlife|labuan island ww2|sabah malaysia
description:
First of all where is Labuan and why we went there?
Labuan is a Malaysian island near Brunei with direct ferry connections between both Brunei and Kota Kinabalu (Sabah, Malaysia), many people recommended us to stay on the island as we were going to get a boat from Brunei to Kota Kinabalu and the only way to go from Brunei to KK by boat is to stop in Labuan first and then get another ferry. 
We decided to take the ferry because we wanted to avoid the bus ride as it passes to multiple states of Malaysia and Brunei meaning that every time we enter a different state or country we get a stamp and at this point we don't have many pages on our passport left, so the boat was our best option. So we decided to stay a couple of nights in Labuan. The ferry from Brunei to Labuan takes about one and a half hours and then the other ferry from Labuan to KK takes 3/4 hours. 
Anyway, we stayed in Labuan with a local Filipina - Luz, Luz and her friend toured us around the island and showed us the points of interest, there's not a lot to do unless you want to go to have some beers and enjoy the sun and beaches, so we recommend only a day or two to explore the island, also it's not easy to get around if you don't have a car, mopeds are expensive and local transports don't exist (at least we didn't find any).
Hope you enjoy the video and let us know if we missed something on this Island.

description:
We’ve always wanted to come to Borneo since the first time we landed in Malaysia last year. We didn’t make back then but we made it happen this time and here we are. 
Borneo is the third largest island in the world and it’s divided into 3 different countries - Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei. Borneo has the most beautiful rainforests we’ve ever seen and a great variety of animals inhabiting them. Some of the rainforests have been destroyed for the palm oil extraction and the government of the three countries have been working on it trying to preserve what’s left now. 
But let’s not talk about that for now, right now we are staying in Kuching and the vibe here is different from peninsular Malaysia, people are extremely friendly and welcoming and even though it’s a big city it doesn’t feel like it everyone is so chilled and the traffic, if we can call it traffic, it’s barely inexistente.

We spent 3 days and 2 nights in Khuri desert and it couldn't have been a better experience just the 4 of us, the camels and the nature surrounding us. We had to opportunity to visit a few remote villages and to see a few wild animals (gazelles, lizzards, eagles and many different types of birds) hence the name safari desert tour.
We would like to shout out a special thanks to Ali and Kato for making our experience even more memorable, and if you are heading to Jaisalmer and are interested in something like this we will leave their contacts below.

description:
We started in Goa to have a smooth start in India and we highly recommend doing this as India can be quiet intense and we don't want you to arrive is Delhi or another big city and disliking the country straightaway like many people who disregard this advice, India is a lovely country you just have to learn how to travel whilst there.   
Anyway, we stayed in Agonda Beach which is south of Goa for a week, just relaxing and slowing getting adapted to this massive country. We are very exited to show you guys what we have been up to. India is crazy and full of life, we decided to stay for two months so don't miss the next vlog.

About Agonda: it's very quiet most of the backpackers stay in North Goa for the parties, it's not difficult to find cheap places to eat or stay but the prices are a bit higher compared to other areas of Goa.

description:
Despite having beautiful, tranquil, peaceful beaches, Gili Trawangan is for the most part, a party island. For the tiny island that it is, it is packed full of international tourists.

However, Gili T, as it’s otherwise known, has developed into much more over the recent years. The east side of the island (where the boat drops you off) is the most developed, with loads of restaurants, bars, accommodation and diving schools and it is here that most of the party goers reside. The west side is relatively quiet with luxury resorts and not much else, but great for a family holiday or a romantic getaway. The north and south ends are a little closer to the action without being right in the thick of it, and the south end in particular has some nice accommodation options here.

The island is tiny. You can walk around the entire island in about 2hrs, or ride your bike around it. There is no motored transport on the island, only walk, bicycle or cidomo.

Supertree Grove consists of 18 fantastic supertrees that act as vertical gardens. These structures aren’t exactly real trees, but rather a series of man-made frames that support tropical flowers, ferns and other plants, forming a lush, colorful skin. With otherworldly design features, this garden is unlike any you have seen before.
hese tree-like structures are fitted with environmental technologies that mimic the functions of regular trees, such as solar photo-voltaic systems that convert sunlight into energy, just like how trees photosynthesize; and collection of rainwater for use in irrigation and fountain displays, exactly like how trees absorb rainwater for growth. description:
We rented a scooter and headed to the Tegallalang rice terraces as they are one of the most iconic attractions in Bali. 
The rice terraces at Tegallalang are said to embody the traditional farming ways of the Balinese people and still use the traditional Balinese irrigation system of Subak.
When we arrived we were greeted by a guide who showed us the cinnamon plant, natural cocoa and the civets (the animals used to produce luwak coffee), we also had the pleasure to try a few different types of tea and coffee offered by the guide.

After spending more than we anticipated exploring the rice terraces, we had a delicious smoothie fruit bowl for lunch in Ubud and headed to Campuhan Ridge Walk to see the sunset, Campuhan Ridge Walk is a paved trail through Campuhan Ridge and it's a free and easy nature trek, specially for those in love with nature.

This is what we cover in this video, if you enjoyed it please give it a thumbs up and leave a comment and if you haven't done it yet: subscribe to our channel.
Thanks for watching and see you guys on the next one... Goodbye!

A few weeks ago, after visiting Ho Chi Minh city, we went to our next destination: Mui Ne. No high expectations about the this place and... wow, we were so impressed, not by the beach as Mui Ne is known by it’s beach, water sports and resorts, but by the surroundings 🤗. There is so much you can explore in Mui Ne: the white and red sand dunes, being the white located 25km outside Mui Ne and the red 8km. There is also the fishermen village, the fairy stream which is a long narrow flow of water surrounded by red sand dunes and nature, breathtaking views 💛. 
We did it all and below are a few pictures of our visit.

title: Argao Cebu’s Secret Spanish Town: The One with Historic Ruins & Sights!
tags: Argao Cebu|Argao Cebu travel vlog|Southern Cebu hidden gems|Things to do in Argao Cebu|Cebu tourist spots|historic spanish town cebu|Argao spanish colonial sites|old spanish ruins philippines|Cebu heritage tour|Argao church cebu|Cebu secret spots|Argao sightseeing guide|historical places in cebu|exploring argao town|Southern Cebu road trip itinerary|Argao Cebu's Secret Spanish Town
description:
"Welcome to Argao, a beautifully preserved historic Spanish town in Southern Cebu that remains a total hidden gem. Known as the destination with magnificent stone ruins and colonial sights, this is a side of Cebu most tourists never get to see."

We explore the historic heritage town of Argao in southern Cebu, Philippines, featuring iconic Spanish-colonial landmarks like the centuries-old St. Michael the Archangel Parish Church, the Cabecera de Argao complex, and the historic watchtower (Baluarte).

We visit Town of Argao and The Archdiocesan Shrine of Saint Michael the Archangel, famously known as the Argao Old Church, anchors the Cabecera de Argao, which is widely recognized as one of the most well-preserved Spanish colonial heritage sites in southern Cebu. As a designated National Cultural Treasure, this entire Argao historical landmark and stone church complex provides definitive insight into 18th-century Philippine ecclesiastical architecture and fortified defensive structures.

Directly adjacent to the parish stands the town’s ancient defensive pueblo network. The historic compound incorporates the Casa Real (the old municipal hall), the Argao Hall of Justice, and a expansive central plaza area known as Unity Plaza. Intact military infrastructure still defines the perimeter, including the massive Puerta Marina stone gateway and strategically placed antique defensive cannons. Additional features of the complex include the 18th-century Capilla Mortuario—which historically functioned as a mortuary chapel and isolated leprosarium—and the Museo de la Parroquia de San Miguel, which securely protects a vast collection of centuries-old liturgical artifacts and parish records.

title: Anda Town Bohol, Leaving Paradise - The One Going Back To Cebu
tags: Anda Bohol travel vlog|Quinale Beach Bohol|leaving Anda Bohol trip|bus ride from Anda to Tagbilaran|Bohol countryside travel|Tagbilaran to Cebu ferry|Anda Bohol hidden gem|quiet beaches in Bohol|undeveloped beaches Philippines|Anda to Tagbilaran route|Bohol island travel guide|Cebu to Bohol boat ride|peaceful beach destinations|Anda Bohol tourism|scenic travel Philippines|Couples in Anda bohol|Anda bohol for couples|Best bohol travel for couples
description:
Leaving stunning Coastal Town of Anda Bohol and the beautiful Quinale Beach behind, we embark on a scenic bus trip from Anda Bohol, we take you along the beautiful eastern coast. Watch the island scenery unfold as we highlight the best roadside sights on the way back from paradise! 

Today we are Leaving Anda, Bohol. A short final look at one of the Philippines’ most peaceful coastal towns before beginning the scenic journey back to Tagbilaran and onward to Cebu. The ride out of Anda passes quiet villages, coconut-lined roads, and long stretches of untouched coastline that highlight why this region remains one of Bohol’s most beautiful and undeveloped destinations. With fewer tourists and a slower pace of life, Anda feels like a hidden world — and that calm follows you as the bus winds through the countryside toward the port.

The bus ride to Tagbilaran is smooth and filled with views of rural landscapes, Old Spanish homes and churches, and glimpses of the sea. description:
Lumphini Park is nestled in the heart of Bangkok’s bustling Pathum Wan district, it's 142-acre green oasis offers locals and tourists a peaceful escape from city life. Known as “Bangkok’s Central Park,” it features serene lakes, jogging paths, paddle boats, and shaded walkways.

But what truly sets Lumphini apart is Its wild residents—giant monitor lizards. They often reach up to 3 meters in length, roam freely around the park’s lakes and trees. Despite their intimidating size, they’re generally harmless if left undisturbed. You can often spot them sunbathing, swimming, or casually crossing paths with joggers.

Just minutes from Lumphini Park is Chulalongkorn University. It stands as Thailand’s oldest and most prestigious academic institution and offers a vibrant campus life within walking distance of the park

Welcome to Maeklong Railway Market. If you've never seen a train drive straight through a busy market then this is the place to go.

Discover the jaw-droppingly crazy spectacle of Maeklong Railway Market, one of Thailand’s most iconic and thrilling attractions! Located just outside Bangkok, this bustling market is famously built directly on active train tracks. title: Cu Chi Tunnels, Ho Chi Minh City - The One Beneath The Jungle
tags: Cu Chi Tunnels Vietnam history tour|guided tour of Cu Chi Tunnels from Ho Chi Minh City|Vietnam War tunnels near Saigon|Cu Chi Tunnels entrance fee and hours|how to get to Cu Chi Tunnels from Ho Chi Minh|Cu Chi Tunnels group tour for tourists|Cu Chi Tunnels war museum highlights|Cu Chi Tunnels underground bunker tour|Cu Chi Tunnels shooting range experience|Cu Chi Tunnels day trip from Saigon|Cu Chi Tunnels Ho Chi Minh|Ho Chi Minh Tunnels|Saigon War Tunnels
description:
Cu Chi Tunnels is an unforgettable experience that offers a deep dive into Vietnam’s wartime history and resilience. Located just 60 km northwest of Ho Chi Minh City, this vast underground network played a crucial role during the Vietnam War, serving as a strategic base for the Viet Cong. Today, it's one of Vietnam’s top tourist attractions, drawing history buffs, adventure seekers, and curious travelers alike.

Touring the Cu Chi Tunnels allowed us to crawl through narrow passageways, witness hidden trapdoors, and explore underground bunkers, kitchens, and command centers. Our guide provided fascinating insights into guerrilla warfare tactics and the daily life of soldiers who lived and fought from beneath the earth. The site also features interactive exhibits, weapon displays, and even the chance to fire authentic war-era rifles,  including the legendary Ak47 at a nearby shooting range.

Come along and join us as we squeeze our way through the narrow tunnels on our hands and knees.

Today Rona and myself headed out to downtown Cebu, where we visit a few historical and famous Spanish sites and enjoy some delicious street food. Downtown Cebu boasts a treasure trove of historical Spanish sites that offer glimpses into its colonial past:

Magellan’s Cross: Iconic symbol of Christianity in Cebu; planted by Portuguese explorer Ferdinand Magellan in 1521; housed in a small chapel near the Basilica; vibrant murals depicting its installation.

Basilica Minore del Santo Niño: Oldest Roman Catholic church in the Philippines; founded in 1565; home to the revered Santo Niño statue; Baroque architecture; significant religious site.

Fort San Pedro: Spanish-era military defense structure; triangular shape; built in 1738; constructed under Miguel López de Legazpi’s rule; stone walls; lush garden surroundings.

Colon Street: Oldest street in the Philippines; named after Christopher Columbus; established in 1565; bustling area for trade and commerce; historical landmarks nearby; vibrant cultural heritage.

Casa Gorordo Museum: 19th-century house; displays colonial-era artifacts; showcases the lifestyle of prominent Filipino-Spanish families; restored architectural features; charming garden area.

Parian District: Historical hub for Chinese and Spanish mestizos; significant trade center during the Spanish era; old houses; The Jesuit House and Yap-Sandiego Ancestral House located here.

Cebu Metropolitan Cathedral: Grand Spanish-era cathedral; seat of the Archdiocese of Cebu; classical facade; religious art and historical exhibits; serene gardens.

These sites weave a fascinating narrative of Cebu's Spanish colonial history through their architecture, culture, and enduring significance.

Our Last day in Camiguin and we went on another scooter adventure (whilst Rona Sang) to the famous Hibok Hibok-Ardent Hot Spring. Sadly and very disappointedly the water was a joke, not too cold but just bearable, even though the a sign outside said water temperature was 37 degrees. So not hot by any stretch of the imagination. Felt like a normal mountain river stream. We made the best of it anyway and enjoyed time relaxing our aching muscles from previous days. There are many other hot springs on Camiguin Island and also a dedicated cold spring, not to be confused with ours, lol.

Later we went searching for lanzonies in the town market which we finally found by the roadside on the way back to our hotel, and they were so delicious and sweet.  Fyi, lanzonies are the icon fruit of Camiguin. We also took time to explore a bit of the local market and town of Mambajao, the capital of Camiguin. We were amazed and a little shocked to stumble across an old payphone. It's the first I've seen in the Philippines and the first Rona has ever seen in her life. There are also some amazing old ancestral homes towards the market area as well as the very famous by Vjandep Bakery. They make another of Camiguin's famous food icons in the absolutely deliciously sweet Pastels, which we bought 2 boxes of to enjoy. After taking a look at some of the ancestral homes we stop by Viola's, famous for having one of -if not the best Halo halo in Camiguin. We finished the day with our third visit to a local Italian restaurant for an amazing pizza and shake.

Our final day was up very early to eat breakfast near the airport before our flight back to Cebu. Camiguin Island is such an amazing place.

White Island, an uninhabited sandbar off the coast of Camiguin, is a gem of natural beauty. This picturesque crescent-shaped paradise, known for its powdery white sand and crystal-clear waters, attracts tourists and nature lovers alike. Situated near the town of Mambajao, the island offers stunning panoramic views of Mount Hibok-Hibok, a nearby stratovolcano, and the surrounding landscape. Visitors can enjoy a short boat ride from Barangay Yumbing to reach this tranquil haven, usually around 10 minutes, making it an accessible getaway.

One of the most captivating features of White Island is its unspoiled and untouched environment. The island's powdery white sand and pristine waters provide the perfect setting for various activities such as snorkeling, swimming, and sunbathing. With its vibrant marine life, snorkeling around White Island is a must-do for underwater enthusiasts. Due to the lack of permanent structures, visitors are encouraged to bring essentials like sunscreen, hats or caps, umbrellas, snacks, water, and picnic mats to fully enjoy their time on the sandbar.

The best time to visit White Island is during the dry season, from February to May, when the weather is ideal for outdoor activities. Early morning visits between 5:00 AM and 7:00 AM are recommended to avoid the heat and crowds, while late afternoon visits between 3:00 PM and 5:00 PM also offer a pleasant experience. It is essential to bring sunscreen to protect against the strong sun, as there is no shade on the island. Umbrellas and hats or caps are useful for keeping cool, and visitors should not forget to pack snacks and water, as there are no facilities on the island.

For those who love photography, bringing a camera to capture the stunning scenery and memories is a must. Additionally, picnic mats can make relaxing on the sand more comfortable, and snorkel gear is recommended for exploring the underwater world. Life jackets are available for rent, especially useful for those who are not strong swimmers.

To access White Island, visitors must pay a small entrance fee, usually around 50 pesos, and a boat fee for the round trip, typically around 550 pesos. Despite these minimal costs, the experience of visiting White Island is priceless. As a popular tourist attraction in Camiguin, this natural beauty remains a favorite destination for travelers seeking a tropical paradise.

White Island is a testament to the natural beauty and charm of the Philippines. Its unspoiled environment, vibrant marine life, and breathtaking views make it a must-visit destination for anyone traveling to Camiguin. Whether you are looking for relaxation, adventure, or simply a picturesque spot to soak in the beauty of nature, White Island has it all.

This is Rona's first visit to Boracay Island and my third, but it's been around 10 years since the last time I was here. A lot has changed in the past decade, however Boracay Island is just as beautiful, exciting and fun as it was all those years ago. There's wonderful food, great night life, powdery white sand and warm turquoise water, so who could wish for anymore?

Come along as I share our walks around Boracay island highlighted by it's magnificent beaches, huge variety of food, the always entertaining Dmall and the many colourful market stalls along it's kilometres long beachfront.
